speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEVELOPMENTS AT UN SPECIAL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to report to the house on the emergency special session of the general assembly which last evening adopted by unanimous vote a draft resolution submitted yesterday by ten Arab delegations, including those of Lebanon, Jordan and the United Arab Republic. The resolution welcomes assurances given by the Arab states that they would respect each other's systems of government in accordance with provisions of the pact of the league of Arab states, and calls upon all member states to observe certain principles of international behaviour endorsed by the Afro-Asian conference at Bandung in 1955.
The Canadian government regards the outcome of the session that concluded last evening as satisfactory. The resolution in question follows very closely the text of the earlier seven-power draft resolution of which Canada was a co-sponsor. The Arab resolution requests the secretary general to make such practical arrangements as would adequately help in upholding the purposes and principles of the United Nations charter in relation to Lebanon and Jordan and thereby facilitate the early withdrawal of foreign troops from those two countries.
The new element in the Arab proposal is the reference to facilitating the withdrawal of troops. My understanding is that the formula employed is acceptable to the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States. The resolution, as in the case of the seven-power proposal, also invites the secretary general to continue with steps toward the establishment of an Arab development institution and to report to the general assembly not later than the last day of September of this year.
The Canadian government not only supported this resolution but agreed that it
should have priority over the seven-power draft, which we regarded as a point of departure or basis for discussion for the accomplishment, under United Nations auspices, of an end to inter-Arab rivalries in a form to which all Arabs could subscribe, and in general as a reasonable formula to cover the question of withdrawal and a new approach to the economic problem of the Middle East.
While the resolution is a regional solution for a regional problem, its terms permit a continuing link between the United Nations and future economic and political developments in that area. It should ensure that the cordial relations now established among the Arab states will be carried forward into their individual and collective relations with non-Arab states of the region. The reference in the seven-power draft to a United Nations stand-by force, which received general support from all sections of the house, has been dropped, but I expect that this phase will be given further study at the next session of the general assembly.
To sum up, we have supported this resolution as meeting the essential requirements of a satisfactory conclusion of the discussions in the general assembly. We supported it because of the prospect it affords for peace in the Middle East. The resolution is good as far as it goes, but of course any success in carrying it out will depend upon the further co-operation of the interested countries themselves.
I think it will be generally agreed that once again the United Nations has shown its capacity to deal with crises by the process of reconciliation through negotiation. It is to be hoped that the same spirit will be apparent in the attitude of these states whose co-operation the secretary general will be seeking in the visit to the Middle East which he is about to undertake.

I understand we will have an opportunity to debate this matter, when dealing with the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, but I think we can share the Prime Minister's careful satisfaction at the unanimous passing of a resolution of this kind. It

Canadian Citizenship Act is, after all, satisfying and usually very surprising when any resolution at the United Nations passes unanimously.
I have not had the opportunity, nor have other members had the opportunity, to compare the Arab resolution which was passed unanimously with that of the seven powers, of which Canada was one. I gather that the main difference, however-and perhaps this is of some importance-is that the Arab resolution does make specific reference to the withdrawal of British and United States forces, while the seven-power resolution did not make that specific reference.
This resolution unanimously adopted by the assembly does present at least an opportunity for the finding of a solution to the problems in the Middle East, and we all welcome that. But as I said earlier, there will be an opportunity to discuss this whole question of the work of the general assembly when we have the privilege tomorrow of discussing his estimates with the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the primary purpose of this bill is to remove certain discriminations which now exist against other than natural-born Canadian citizens in relation to loss of Canadian citizenship and, in addition, to make it clear that a person who does not take the oath of allegiance in good faith at the time of acquiring Canadian citizenship is liable to have his Canadian citizenship revoked, subject to the right of such person to a hearing before a commission or court as provided by the act. speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monieith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before discussing the matter at hand I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to an event of great significance to the health of people throughout the world. I refer to the recent commemoration of the tenth anniversary of the founding of the world health organization. This historic milestone in international co-operation was marked by a special session of the world health assembly held in May of this year at Minneapolis. As Minister of National Health and Welfare I was privileged to represent Canada on this occasion, accompanied by a distinguished delegation of Canadian health experts.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Immediately following the commemorative session the eleventh regular world health assembly was convened. My deputy, Dr. G. D. W. Cameron, led the Canadian delegation at these meetings and was ably assisted by three other outstanding health experts, Dr. Arthur Kelly, general secretary of the Canadian Medical Association, Dr. Jules Gilbert, president of the Canadian Public Health Association, and Dr. R. D. Defries, recently retired director of the Connaught medical research laboratories.
The main task of this assembly was to approve WHO's program and budget for 1959, the latter calling for an expenditure of nearly $15 million. While this amount is three times the organization's first budget, I am sure the committee will agree that it is a modest sum in terms of the tremendous job to be done. It is obvious that in large areas of the world, climatic and economic factors have combined to render extremely difficult the attainment of health standards comparable to those we enjoy here in Canada. Yet despite the obstacles, significant progress has been made through the efforts of WHO in co-operation with other international and national agencies both public and private.
As examples of the advances made during the past ten years through the auspices of WHO the following might be mentioned: over half the estimated 50 million persons suffering from yaws have been treated and cured, with the stage now being set for the complete eradication of this disease in the next few years; several hundred thousand children have received B.C.G. vaccine as a protection against tuberculosis; substantial assistance has been given toward the training of doctors, nurses and other health personnel and opportunities provided for these individuals to go abroad for the study of the technical and administrative aspects of health service administration; and finally, WHO has recently embarked on its most ambitious project, the world-wide eradication of malaria over the next ten years.
These are but a few highlights of the work performed by WHO during its first decade. I am sure all hon. members recognize the importance of its activities not only in helping secure healthier, happier and more productive lives for millions of the world's peoples but also in furthering the cause of peace and understanding among nations. I feel that I spoke for Canadians everywhere when I told the tenth anniversary session that "as WHO enters its second decade, we pledge our continuing and wholehearted support to what we consider is one of the most outstanding experiments in international co-operation ever undertaken".

Supply-Health and Welfare
I want to turn now to the subject of our deliberations today, the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the fiscal year 1958-59. In this period we are budgeting for a total outlay of $1,180,089,181, the highest level of expenditure in the department's history. Of this over-all amount no less than 92 per cent covers statutory items including some $555 million to be expended from the old age security fund. Only $93,272,181 or 8 per cent of the total estimated outlay represents items to be voted by the house.
As a whole, these estimates embody an increase of $184,004,297 over our expectations for the past fiscal year. A full 92.5 per cent of this increase is taken up by statutory items reflecting recent amendments to Canada's major welfare legislation. To be specific, a projected rise of $33,235,000 in family allowance payments is due to a general increase in population as well as to changes in rates of benefit which became effective last September; an increase of $117,464,000 in old age security payments stems chiefly from the new $55 a month level in benefits effective last November; a similarly increased level in maximum benefits largely accounts for the expected rise of $5,700,000 in old age assistance payments, $6,200,000 in disabled persons' allowances, and $700,000 in blind persons' allowances. Finally, an estimated increase of nearly $7 million in expenditures under the unemployment assistance program is due for the most part to the removal of the threshold on federal participation and the entry of Ontario and Nova Scotia into the scheme.
So much for the increase in so far as statutory items are concerned. The remaining 7.5 per cent of the increase in our over-all expenditures pertains to items to be voted by the house. A large proportion of this additional outlay of $13,830,297 relates to the national health program, and particularly to the recent changes in the hospital construction grant which I announced to the house last December.
In this connection, hon. members may recall that the grant basis of $1,000 per unit for active treatment beds or "bed equivalents" and $1,500 per unit for chronic, convalescent, mental and tuberculosis beds was raised to $2,000 per unit. In addition, the allowance for beds in nurses' residences was upped from $500 to $750 per unit, and the latter assistance applied for the first time to beds in internes' quarters. A further new departure under the hospital construction grant was the allotment of $4 million for major renovation projects.
Another significant increase in non-statutory items which I might mention is the additional $1,644,450 earmarked in the two votes for
TMr. Monteith (Perth).]
northern health services. This represents primarily provision for the completion of the new Whitehorse hospital and for its staffing and equipment. Also covered in the increment is the transfer to northern health services of 17 organized field units in the territories formerly operated by Indian health services, and the continuation of construction of a new departmental hospital at Aklavik.
Hon. members will note that the department's 1958-59 estimates do not include provision for federal contributions to provincial hospital insurance and diagnostic services programs. Projected figures in this connection were not available when the main estimates were drawn up, and it is not the custom to provide for statutory items in the supple-mentaries. While government expenditures with respect to provincial plans will be provided for in next year's main estimates, the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act lays down that federal payments are to be a direct charge on the consolidated revenue fund and can thus be made despite the lack of an estimates item.
I might say here that we expect federal outlays on the hospital insurance program to be something less than $70 million for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1959. This will apply to the five provincial plans operating as of July 1, 1958, and those additional plans which it is hoped will get under way as of January 1, 1959.
These, then, are the main items of the projected expenditures of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I will, of course, be happy to answer questions which hon. members may have on the various items.
Before I take my seat, Mr. Chairman, I would like to thank all members of the staff of my department for their loyal co-operation and assistance during the past year. I think it is appropriate that I should mention that it is exactly a year since I was sworn in as minister of this department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we listened with great interest to the remarks of the minister. I think the committee might expect there would be a pretty thorough discussion of these estimates at the present sitting, because I believe we have had no discussion of this very important and large department since 1956. It is true that at that time the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare were reviewed by the estimates committee.
I found, in endeavouring to keep up to date with the department's activities, that it was rather difficult because the last annual report seems to be dated March 31, 1956. I must suggest to the minister that it is not very helpful to the committee of supply

when annual reports are so out of date. Perhaps he might just indicate to the committee when he thinks the annual report for the year ended March 31, 1957 might become available.
I join with the minister in his commendation of the activities of the world health organization. I think we as Canadians are particularly interested in the tenth anniversary activities of this organization because it is an outstanding Canadian and member of the Department of National Health and Welfare who has the honour of being president of this world organization this year. The minister has a great galaxy of talent around him.
We as Canadians are proud also of the fact that his deputy minister on the welfare side was honoured this year by being chosen to preside over the economic and social committee of the United Nations when it met in Geneva. Of course all of us are very familiar with the outstanding talents of the two fine people who are in front of the minister at the moment. One is a lady who has the honour of being the first lady to appear in this house in the role of adviser to the committee of supply and to her minister. As the minister has indicated, Dr. Cameron was head of the delegation that attended the world health organization this year, and his reputation is very wide indeed as an outstanding public health administrator.
The only item that has had any careful review by a committee of this house since 1956 is the item in this year's estimates with respect to civil defence, item No. 256. The minister was exceedingly cautious in giving the estimates committee very much information as to future plans in this respect. He always indicated that as General Graham was about-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I just point out that I propose to have something to say when we do come to the civil defence item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That will be very welcome, Mr. Chairman, because we feel that we could learn so little about the future because of the fact that the minister repeatedly said that the subjects the committee on estimates was interested in were going to be referred to General Graham. I think we all look forward to General Graham's study. In the estimates committee I did urge the minister to impress on General Graham the desirability of not having one of those long drawn out investigations if it could be avoided, in view of the seriousness of the problem of civil defence and, as the committee on estimates pointed out, the necessity for co-ordination and co-operation
Supply-Health and Welfare among civil defence organizations, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of National Defence.
I hope when the minister does report to us with respect to civil defence he will report upon the information that was given to us by the Prime Minister concerning mass evacuation plans, as well as the plans for the erection of shelters and matters of that kind. This is something which I believe is probably foremost in the thinking of the people of Canada today when they regard the question of civil defence. We are all exceedingly alarmed about the consequences of these awful weapons that have been developed.
With respect to new planning for our defence, we have for some time heard largely from certain left-wing elements that probably did not get the attention they deserved. I think we can find a pretty universal feeling registered with respect to this matter, when we consider that no less than the Financial Post last week put as graphically as I think anybody has to date the seriousness of our defence planning.
In its lead editorial on August 16 the Financial Post had this to say, and I think it relates to the question of civil defence as it does to defence policy generally. I am only going to read some excerpts, but the heading of the editorial was "There is No Such Thing as Adequate Defence". It went on to say:
It is absolute and utter folly for our leaders to try to make the public believe there is safety.
We may have all the defence machinery we are willing to pay for. But that is about all we have. And not even doubling or tripling our defence expenditure will give us real security. Nor will gigantic defence and bomb shelter programs.
The article goes on to point out the awful havoc that resulted from the atom bombing of Japan. This certainly shook and impressed me very much indeed. It is reported that of 32,000 children born in Hiroshima not less than 5,000, almost one in six, were deformed or stillborn. This figure includes 1,100 with skeletal deficiencies or serious muscular weaknesses; almost 100 with deformed brains or without brains altogether; almost 200 without lips and the same number without sexual organs; 25 with one eye or no eyes and 4 lacking even eye-openings. This is a report from a recent investigation of atomic bomb fall-out in Japan. Today's bombs, as we all know, are about 1,000 times more deadly than those of Hiroshima. This is the caution of the Financial Post; that our planet could tolerate war as an instrument of national policy when war was a little thing like world war I or II, but it cannot do so any longer.
We, I think, are exceedingly proud to have in Canada at the moment the tenth annual conference of geneticists, who are meeting in

Supply-Health and Welfare Montreal. I was astounded to ascertain that these scientists will have read to them no less than 590 papers, some of which of course will relate to the problems and worries I have just described, this question of the effect of radiation on genetics, even the current effect of radiation from fall-out drift.
I believe that in 1955 the former minister of national health and welfare indicated to a conference of experts on this subject that the minister's department was giving careful consideration to all the elements connected with this ghastly problem. I wonder if later on in the debate the minister would give us some information about what has developed in the department since 1955 in keeping abreast with this problem of radiation. It is a subject that has had very considerable debate in the parliament of the United Kingdom. I think it is most appropriate that we in this house be brought up to date, not only on the effect of fall-out drift but also the best information that is available to the department to date with respect to the predicted effect on genetics as a whole.
As the minister has indicated, there has been a remarkable growth indeed in the importance of the role of the Department of National Health and Welfare across the country. I believe that in the parliament buildings at Fredericton, New Brunswick there is a cairn of which they are very proud because it honours the fact that New Brunswick appointed the first minister of health in the British Empire.
It is remarkable to note just within how many years health has become an important government function. I think the first public health laboratory in North America was developed in Ontario as recently as 1890. About that time I think the total expenditure of the province of Ontario with respect to all health functions was about $4,000, largely for a part-time secretary and some help to the secretary. In Ontario alone I would imagine that the health budget today exceeds $60 million, and I think the administration employs some 6,000 or 7,000 people.
In our own department, as the minister has indicated, there has been a terrific growth. He points out that the estimates before us today amount to $1,200 million. He of course has pointed out, as the Minister of Finance indicated in his budget, that it will be necessary to provide additionally about $70 million for our participation to the end of this fiscal year in the new hospitalization scheme. I had the honour to be one of the federal representatives attending the preliminary conferences with the provinces in 1955 and 1956, and on the basis 
of full participation it was calculated that the federal cost would be in the neighbourhood of $200 million.
As the minister has indicated, only five provinces to date have accepted this offer. My own province, the largest in the land, will become a participant from January 1, 1959. I am hoping that this scheme will have universal acceptance in the not too distant future. I think most of us are particularly concerned about the other large province, namely the province of Quebec; and perhaps the minister could indicate to us just what possibility there is of that province entering into the hospitalization scheme in the near future. The taxpayers of that province, of course, are obliged to contribute to federal taxation, and it seems a pity that that government is not moving very fast to provide to the people of that province the benefits of this additional advance in the health sphere which was introduced by the former administration and which the minister is proceeding with, I know, with great interest and support.
Also, Mr. Chairman, I believe we should like to have a little report from the minister with respect to our Salk vaccine program. I think we all realize that there have been remarkable results from the program that was introduced. Some statistics were tabled in this house, I think it was late last session, which indicated a remarkable decline in the incidence of this dread disease; and I think great credit is attributed to the vaccine that was developed. In fact progress has gone so far that those concerned with the very important campaign for the elimination of poliomyelitis in the United States, which raised tremendous sums of money from the public in the past, through the march of dimes and so on with which we are all familiar-I believe were of opinion that they had recently reached a point of correction and almost of control of this particular threat to health to the extent that they felt they could turn their efforts from polio to the other very dread health threat area, namely that of the arthritic and rheumatic sufferers.
I wonder whether the minister would also indicate to us during the course of our discussion in this committee something about the advances that have taken place in the field of cancer research since we last had the opportunity of examining his predecessor. I believe that under the health program the department, as well as concentrating on cancer research, is giving special concentration in the field of mental diseases. I think it is shocking to us all to be told, as I say, that there are perhaps more hospital beds today occupied by sufferers from mental disease than by sufferers in all the other

general hospitals put together. It seems to me something that is growing at an alarming pace. I think the committee would be exceedingly interested in getting from the minister an up to date report upon the co-operative efforts of his department in association with the provinces in this particular field.
On the estimates before us there is, of course, an opportunity for almost unlimited discussion on matters in which all members of the house are particularly interested. Sometimes we have in committee of supply items with which only a limited number of our membership are familiar with or in which they have a particular interest. But when we realize that in committee this morning we are discussing such matters of wide public political and human interest as family allowances, health insurance, disability pensions, blind pensions and so on, I think we realize that at this stage it is difficult to confine oneself to inquiries that will simply bring out new information and not necessarily be repetitious.
With respect to health insurance, either now or on the item in the estimates I should like to obtain from the minister some information as to which of the provinces seem to be adopting a policy under which there will be, shall I say, a discouragement of putting in the hospitals people who could very well get laboratory X-ray and other services under this scheme without actual admittance to hospital. I feel that if this procedure is not encouraged, our hospitals will simply have a burden upon them of people who do not need to be actually in a hospital but who will demand from their physician admission to a hospital simply because of the free services and so on that might not otherwise be provided in consequence of this national plan.
I have been talking to some doctor friends of mine in the past. I know they at all times feel they must be conscientious, but I understand that the pressure upon them is something fearsome. One can understand that when one realizes that it is more or less left to them to decide. The doctor must recommend that a patient go to a hospital or otherwise in order to get the benefits of the insurance provisions that are now available. I think this is a very important matter, and we would like to know about the various provincial schemes in this regard. Naturally we would like to know whether or not there is any change in the position of the present administration with respect to including tuberculosis and mental hospitalization costs in the scheme.
My hon. friend's party was certainly very forthright on this subject in the 1957 election
Supply-Health and Welfare campaign, and in Winnipeg on May 14, 1957 the Prime Minister left no doubt as to the position of his party in this respect. He was quoted not only in the Winnipeg Free Press but also in the Tribune as saying the Conservatives would repair a very serious omission in the hospital scheme of the former administration and would include tuberculosis and mental institutions in the sharing arrangement with respect to hospital costs.
A short time later, he just happened to be speaking in Saskatoon at the time of the annual convention of the Canadian Hospital Association, and he repeated this commitment. We all know there was a meeting of the premiers during the following November, but from all we can read it has been indicated that while provincial costs in respect of tuberculosis and mental institutions might be shared by the federal government, if that were done then there would be an equivalent deduction from the general provision somewhere else under the dominion-provincial arrangements.
With respect to our senior citizens, an inquiry was made yesterday about when we might expect to receive the Clark report, which is the result of an investigation which we all know was designed to take a particular look at the United States social welfare provisions in respect of senior citizens. This report, of course, has been much longer delayed than was originally anticipated, and I will not press the minister further on that point because yesterday the hon. member for Welland got some information on the subject from the Prime Minister.
I do think, however, that when we come to the question of old age security we could very profitably discuss such matters as further advances in the development of low rental housing for our aged people. I am very disturbed to read that the governmental institution type of shelter for the aged is proving to be exceedingly expensive. There are a great many people, of course, who are unable to look after themselves or to live in accommodation under their own control, but on the other hand there are many who would probably prefer this class of shelter. It is certainly much more economical to assist and promote individual housing accommodation of better quality for our aged people than to accommodate such people in government sponsored institutions.
I read two or three years ago, for instance, that Lambert House in Toronto was calculated to operate at a cost of about $120 per month per patient, and the costs are probably a great deal higher today. We are all aware that the subsidy available on housing accommodation through Central Mortgage and

Supply-Health and Welfare Housing Corporation is certainly very modest indeed. I believe, therefore, that if there were an increase in the effort to co-operate with the provinces and the municipalities in this field this would have very widespread approval.
I wonder if the minister would tell us during his subsequent remarks something about the situation with respect to the training of nurses in Canada. There is a general feeling that nurses, as a group, bearing in mind the wonderful work they eventually do, probably have a harder time to get their training than any other group who have to have a long term of post-matriculation training before they can qualify in their profession. Could the minister give us some information in that respect?
In conclusion I simply want to say that I think we all agree in this committee that there has been great progress in the health field and indeed in the welfare field. As a result, most of us probably know that a lot more should be done in regard to health protection than we actually are doing. Perhaps the minister will just indicate to us later on whether there have been some new developments or increased efforts with respect to publicity in the promotion of good health in Canada through his department. Is the department today in a position to do very much in the way of advertising or promotional work, or can this only be done through the instrumentality of the provinces?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I have a few remarks to make at this stage. I would like to first compliment the minister and the government on the measures introduced to improve the various health plans and so forth which exist in Canada at the present time which, I might say, are very inadequate. Steps, however, have been taken in the right direction. We in this group do not feel that all the action has been taken which should have been taken, and certainly we feel that the steps which the Conservative party indicated on many occasions it would take, if given the opportunity, should now be taken.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who is the first member of the Liberal party to speak on this matter. One or two of his remarks were significant, first with respect to the increased costs in regard to admission to hospitals and so on, but I feel that this is possibly a matter which could be very well left to the discretion of our doctors and the medical profession generally. My personal experience with doctors has been that they are very responsible professional people, and I do not think there is any danger, certainly no great danger, that this


plan is going to be abused by Canadian medical practitioners. In fact I believe that often in the past it has proved quite a burden to doctors when their patients needed hospital treatment and they realized the patients were not in a financial position to obtain it. I feel thoroughly satisfied, and I think I can speak on behalf of this group in this connection, that we should have confidence in the doctors of our country and that they will not abuse this plan when it comes into effect.
One thing that strikes me and this group is that we seem to have a false sense of values in this country today. We see a lot of propaganda-one could call it that-in the newspapers regarding the terrible burden of cost which any hospital plan or health plan would involve. But if we check the estimates of two very important departments, those of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of National Defence, we find that the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, including the statutory items, amount to just about 60 per cent of what we are expending on defence, and as had been pointed out on many occasions and as was pointed out by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River quoting from the Financial Post, most of this money being spent on defence is wasted because the defence material on which we are spending this money is obsolete before we get it.
Thus I fail to see why we should have such a spotlight on the legitimate costs involved in a matter so important as the nation's health, while at the same time the waste of money on obsolete weapons passes almost without comment. As a particular illustration of this point I might mention that at the present time the government is faced with a decision whether or not to put a certain type of aeroplane into production. If they decide to go ahead the cost involved will amount to $2 million for each plane. This in the aggregate would certainly represent much more than is presently being expended in looking after the health needs of the entire country.
One of the worst omissions of this government is that the vision which some departments seem to show has not been carried into this particular ministry. We see no such willingness on the part of the government to branch out into new fields in the Department of National Health and Welfare as there is, for example, in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. We do not find the drive which has been demonstrated in other fields.

I think this contention can be illustrated by its attitude toward the present hospital plan. All that has been done in the last year or year and a half since this government took over has been to bring in some very minor amendments to a plan which was originally very inadequate. Certainly there has been no sign to date that this government is showing any vision or initiative in developing and planning a health service for this country, although such a plan is badly needed. It is particularly difficult to understand this attitude when we look back over the past few years and note the stand which was taken by some of those who are now cabinet ministers.
This morning, in answer to a question with regard to a bill of rights, the Prime Minister made the statement that the stand of the government now is the same as it was before. I only wish the same thing was true with regard to health insurance and hospital insurance. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River mentioned one particular statement of the Prime Minister as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press. I should like to give another which was reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 28, 1957. It was reported from the Saskatoon meeting held on May 27:
Mr. Diefenbaker reminded that the Conservative party had consistently advocated health insurance-
This is not only a hospitalization plan; it is complete health insurance, a complete hospital and health insurance plan. He went on to say that the Conservative party still believed that hospital insurance should cover patients in mental and tuberculosis institutions.
It has been said during this session that on occasion newspaper reports cannot be relied upon too heavily. But I think one thing we can rely on is our own record in Hansard as it appears from day to day, and we And that on February 16, 1956, at page 1233 of Hansard, the Prime Minister, then the hon. member for Prince Albert, asked the following question:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In the submission of the health plan to the various provinces, were tuberculosis and mental cases included? If not, why were they not included, and is consideration being given thereto?
The answer of the former prime minister was:
They were not included. For many years they have been recognized as a provincial responsibility and the submission that was being made was for the provision of services additional to those already in existence.
Moreover, during the debate on the health insurance bill on April 10, 1957, as reported
Supply-Health and Welfare at page 3385 and subsequent pages of Hansard, again the present Prime Minister said:
Our desire, while giving full support to the legislation as we have throughout, in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton, is to do our part even at this late hour to improve the legislation in order to make it more effective.
And a little later he said:
The amendment moved by the hon. member would refer the bill to the committee of the whole for the purpose of considering this clause, thereby giving an opportunity, even at this late hour, of including within the ambit of the legislation sanatoria, tuberculosis hospitals and institutions and hospitals for the mentally ill. While tuberculosis is in recession, mental diseases are on the increase.
Further on in the debate the present Prime Minister had this to say:
The goal that all of us have in mind will not be achieved until the two types of institutions to which I have made reference are included within the provisions of this legislation.
The Prime Minister was not alone in taking this stand. We find that many other members of the present government put themselves very clearly on record with regard to this matter. For example, as recorded on page 2657 of Hansard of March 25, 1957 the present Minister of Transport said:
The Ontario government also feel that two very important categories of treatment today are those affecting mental and tubercular patients. They feel, and I think quite rightly, that those costs should be shared by the federal government.
And the present Minister of Fisheries had this to say:
As far as the provinces are concerned there is very heavy expenditure in the fields of mental health and tuberculosis and most people feel, and I think correctly so, that these are illnesses which should not be differentiated from general illnesses and that those who suffer from these diseases should reap as much benefit from the scheme as anyone else.
And of course we have quotations from the late Dr. Blair, who at that time was the health expert of the opposition. I believe these quotations have been given before.
One of the most strongly worded statements on this subject was made by the present Minister of Finance, who has contributed many quotable statements to the debates of this house. He moved an amendment on that occasion, and as reported at page 3238 of Hansard of April 8, 1957 he said:
My purpose is to ask the house to refer the bill back to the committee of the whole in order that this same clause which contains this unjustifiably narrow definition of the word 'hospital' may be reconsidered. I put before the house the ground that there can be no justification in good sense or in principle or in humanity or in the existing facts of life as applied to the financial difficulties of the provinces and municipalities of this country, for this government to try to drive a wedge between general hospitals on the one hand and tuberculosis hospitals and sanatoria and hospitals
3938	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare and institutions for the mentally ill on the other hand. It is only by changing the definition that the government proposes in clause 2(e) that this unworthy distinction can be eliminated. I ask the house, therefore, to send this back in order that this clause, unworthy of the Canadian parliament, unworthy of the pretensions of the government that this is a comprehensive scheme, should be reconsidered and that its shortcomings should be remedied and that the scheme should in fact be made what the minister improperly pretends it to be, a comprehensive scheme of hospital insurance.
Certainly the Minister of Finance, who usually expresses himself in definite language, did so on that occasion. At that time he pointed out very clearly the deficiencies in the plan. I am convinced that no one reading his remarks could have received any impression other than that as soon as he had any opportunity of doing something about it the minister would certainly do so. I wonder if the Minister of National Health and Welfare could inform us if by any chance the arguments and criticisms of the Minister of Finance are as strong today as they were then with regard to this matter.
On January 9, 1957 the C.C.F. moved an amendment in the following language:
-and by reason of their failure to announce legislation establishing a comprehensive and nationwide program of health insurance, with provision for provincial participation.
The vote was recorded on January 16, 1957, and the amendment was supported by the present Prime Minister and all the Conservatives in the house on that occasion. The amendment, of course, was defeated by a vote of 135 to 69 as recorded at page 320 of Hansard of that date.
We also find that when the debate was concluded and the vote taken on April 10, 1957 on the amendment moved by the Minister of Finance with regard to this same measure, among the members of the present cabinet who voted for the amendment as reported at pages 3392 and 3393 of Hansard were the hon. member for Three Rivers, the present Solicitor General; the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce; the present Prime Minister; the hon. member for Hamilton West, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; the hon. member for Eglinton, the present Minister of Finance; the hon. member for Kamloops, the present Minister of Justice; the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the present Minister of Public Works; the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, the present Postmaster General; the hon. member for Calgary North, the present Minister of Agriculture; the hon. member for Broadview, the present Minister of Transport; the hon. member for Greenwood, the present Minister without Portfolio; the hon. member for Queens, the present Minister


of Fisheries; and the hon. member for Ontario, the present Minister of Labour. It is worth noting that these hon. gentlemen voted for the amendment on April 10, 1957, two short months before the election that brought them to office.
I wish to illustrate how inadequate the present plan is. I have some figures taken from the health and welfare division of the dominion bureau of statistics which show that patients in mental hospitals constitute 39 per cent of all bed patients in this country and patients in tuberculosis hospitals constitute 7.63 per cent of all bed patients in Canada at this time. Of course that 47 per cent is excluded under the plan at the present time, just as it was excluded by the previous government, when it was criticized so severely and justifiably by those who now sit on the government side of the house.
In 1950 and 1951 the Department of National Health and Welfare conducted a Canadian sickness survey which indicated that hospital patients in this country totalled about
1.350.000.	With 47 per cent of the patients excluded from the plan this means that roughly only 700,000 will be covered by the federal contribution and a total of 650,000 will not be covered. But that is only one small part of the health picture in Canada. According to the same survey the number of people needing physicians' services that year was
5.950.000.	The number of people requiring dental treatment was two million. The number of people requiring operations was 500,000. The number of people requiring eyeglass examinations was 450,000. The number requiring miscellaneous health care was 200,000. As far as that portion of the plan to which the federal government contributes is concerned we find that a total of only 700,000 patients out of a total of 10,450,000 patients will be covered, or in other words one out of every 15 patients.
Furthermore, an examination of statistics compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics indicates that the population of Canada has increased by 21.4 per cent since 1950. Applying this increase to the survey made in 1950 and 1951 brings the relationship to about one patient out of every 16. I believe that clearly illustrates the inadequacy of this plan. It demonstrates the need on the part of the department to display something of the vision this government is attempting to apply in other fields. There is nothing more important to a country than the health of its citizens.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River dealt with the increasingly important question of radiation poisoning. I too should like the minister to inform the committee just what measures his department is taking to study this matter and what the results of

their investigations reveal. The hon. member also dealt briefly with the question of the United States social security plan, or as we preferred to call it when we have raised this subject on previous occasions, the portable pension plan. We feel this should be part of our social security in Canada. The plan has worked extremely well in the United States, so we are not trail blazing in this regard. We can take lessons from them; we can And out the errors and mistakes they have made over the years, and we can benefit from the experience they have had.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, the need is very great for this department to show much more initiative than it has shown in the past. The country as a whole will be looking for some lead from this government, particularly from this department, which will indicate that the expectations which the people took from the remarks which were made by the members of the present government before it came into power will be realized.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will not delay the committee very long, but I do wish to draw attention to certain other considerations which may have been overlooked by the hon. member for Timmins. I am sure he wants to maintain the fairness for which most members of his group are noted. In his comments concerning the lack of initiative and the lack of new ideas on the part of this department I do not think he took into consideration the rapid strides the department is making in advancing the cause of the health of individuals in the northern parts of Canada. I believe the department is developing very rapidly plans for mobile and quasi-mobile health units in those areas. Perhaps the minister might explain those plans to the members of the committee.
Just briefly in passing, Mr. Chairman, I might also point out that the trend which was followed by the previous administration in this matter of northern health was perhaps not directed along the proper lines. In this regard perhaps the minister might also explain briefly what the departmental plans are concerning the Whitehorse general hospital, its completion and its staffing, as I personally feel that here in this magnificent structure, this magnificent memorial to past Liberal administration, we have our own printing bureau in the Yukon. Perhaps the minister might explain what use is to be made of the buildings which have been constructed in connection with the main hospital facilities.
I would like to express my gratitude and appreciation on behalf of the people of the north for the vision which this government is displaying in its approach to northern health problems. The mobile health units are
Supply-Health and Welfare the only method by which permanent nursing, medical and hospital facilities can be made available to sparsely settled communities. This is a new, a novel idea, an idea which is being vigorously pursued by the present minister.
Knowing that the hon. member for Timmins wants to be fair in a matter of this kind I would suggest that perhaps he should temper the remarks he has just made in the light of this knowledge.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, since its reorganization in 1944 the department has grown very considerably both in size and in importance, as hon. members who have spoken have said. As a matter of fact, today we are being asked to pass estimates for over $1,735 million to be expended in the field of health and welfare in our country. I believe this is a commendable amount of money to be spent in such a good cause, since it represents roughly about one-third of our total budget. However, like most departments with increased responsibilities in recent years, the Department of National Health and Welfare has also become quite complicated and it has been difficult for members to keep up with all the activities that are taking place in the different divisions of the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: A report would help.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Exactly. With annual reports in the past hon. members were able to follow very closely the progress that was being made in the different divisions of the department, and were able to take part in the discussion of the estimates with a clearer understanding of what was going on. But, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has said, this year members do not have an annual report of the department before them. As a matter of fact, as my hon. friend said a moment ago, the last report of the department was tabled by the previous minister of national health and welfare for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1956.
I can quite understand that perhaps we could not expect at this time to have the report for 1958, but I would rather imagine that the report for 1957 should surely be at the disposal of hon. members. I submit, Mr. Chairman, the fact that there is no annual report for 1957 is in direct contravention of section 10 of the Department of National Health and Welfare Act, which states that "the minister shall submit annually a report to parliament in such form as may be prescribed by the governor in council".
When the minister rose to speak a short time ago I expected that he would at least explain to the committee why we have not before us the annual report for 1957. I would

Supply-Health and Welfare have thought that perhaps the minister might have apologized to the house tor having overlooked what not only has been customary in this house and in the Department of National Health and Welfare but for having overlooked something which is a statutory requirement. I submit that this is a very serious omission. It is very serious because the report was not brought down in the first place, and in the second place because neither the minister nor anyone on the government side thought it useful or necessary to advise or explain why there was no report for 1957.
This is a serious omission, but I submit that it becomes more alarming when we consider that in another important department of government it was decided that an annual report would no longer be published and, as a matter of fact, the usual white paper which accompanied the report of that department was completely disregarded.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Almost two-thirds of the expenditures come under those two departments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes. Therefore the very people who accused the previous administration of withholding information from the House of Commons in regard to confidential material are now not only unwilling to produce the confidential document in its 1958 version, but they are not even willing to put at the disposal of hon. members information which is not only useful but necessary, and which was at the disposal of hon. members during the regime of the previous administration when the department was headed by the previous minister of national health and welfare.
The fact that this and several other similar incidents have occurred within recent months is to my mind a far truer measure of the government's solicitude for the rights and privileges of parliament than is the Prime Minister's self-attributed qualification of defender of parliament. I feel it necessary to repeat that in the true interests of the dignity, rights and traditions of this house we have an obligation to look far more carefully at the actions of this government. We could, I feel sure, discredit a good many of the statements we hear concerning the rights of parliament.
In so far as legislation is concerned, I think one of the most remarkable amendments to legislation that was brought forward by this government was the increase from $46 to $55 in the old age pension. I feel quite sure that the increase was indeed welcomed by all citizens, and that the additional $9 was used to very good purpose by a great number of

these recipients. However, I feel it would be wise and useful to at least stop and think about exactly where we are going in the field of social legislation. I am sure all hon. members realize that the natural law, the physical law and the moral law all indicate that no one really gets anything for nothing. It seems to me that we must be ready to pay for whatever we receive. The government's commitment on old age security, which amounts to about $555 million, and other fields of social legislation should be looked at in the light of the deficit of some $1 billion for this year.
Now, as hon. members know these commitments by government are not made on a yearly basis; they are made on a permanent basis. One does not have to be a prophet to forecast deficit budgets for some years to come. I believe, and I do not think anyone would disagree with me, that the national revenue within the next few years will not be sufficiently high to counterbalance the increases in commitments which the government are now making. Unless the government are willing to face very serious economic difficulties, then they will have to consider increasing taxes, no matter how many promises were made to the effect that it was possible to increase social benefits without increasing taxes.
Another thought which I believe is worthy of consideration is that it is not impossible that inflation, even at a time of recession such as we are now having, whether or not we like it, may cut very deeply into the purchasing power of the Canadian public. This may decrease substantially the benefits of the increase in old age security payments, with the result that the very purpose for which the increases were given would be defeated.
In spite of the increase of $9 in the old age security payments I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister did not fulfil the promises he made during the course of the election campaign. In the Toronto Daily Star of April 26, 1957 the following article appeared:
Mr. Diefenbaker condemned the "mean and niggardly" pension increases offered by the Liberal government and said a Conservative administration would deal with the problem more fairly and adequately.
Old age pensions, he promised, would be set "at a figure high enough to meet the needs of our older citizens" and would be adjusted from time to time in accordance with changes in living costs.
Surely the Prime Minister, as well as the hon. members who are now applauding, realizes that $55 a month is not sufficient to meet the needs of our older citizens, nor is the increase of $9 proportionate to the increase in the cost of living in the past few

years. As a matter of fact, if the Prime Minister had fulfilled his promise he would have had to raise the old age security payment to $70 a month. No amount of oratory on the part of the Prime Minister can make the Canadian people believe that the Prime Minister and this government have actually fulfilled the promises made during the election campaign.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Don't be silly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The people were satisfied with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is quite obvious that you cannot make the people believe that, and this is the reason.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We did at the last election.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
You wait until the next one. No matter how much we would like it to be otherwise, in the present stage of our economic development, old age security and other social measures cannot possibly be an end in themselves. They can, at this stage, be only an indefinite form of financial aid which the government may give to certain sectors of our society that need it most, based not on the cost of living, though we would like that to be the case, but based on the capacity of the Canadian economy to pay. I submit that anything above and beyond what the Canadian economy can pay is unrealistic, and is to my mind a dangerous practice which in the end defeats the very purpose for which these social measures were instituted.
I feel sure hon. members will criticize me severely for having said what I have. I shall be considered as rather brutal, but I am sincerely convinced that we must at least realize where we are going and I feel it is my duty to warn the committee of what is happening. I feel that what I say is true, and I feel that eloquent support is given to what I say by the $1 billion deficit for this current fiscal year.
A well balanced social security program also should try to cover as wide a field as possible, so far as our Canadian economy will permit. If it is just and fitting to help our senior citizens, I believe it is equally fitting and right that we should help our junior citizens. I think we, as Canadians and citizens of a new country, should pay particular attention to what we will make of our children. We should do all we can to help families give their children fundamental and minimum standards of food, clothing and schooling in order that they may be able to take part actively, and to the best possible extent, as citizens of this country.
Supply-Health and. Welfare
I do not believe anyone will disagree with that principle. Yet, Mr. Chairman, there was a certain amount of objection, criticism and abuse heaped upon the previous administration when they introduced family allowances. Ever since that time the Conservatives have been extremely cold toward any movement to increase family allowances. At the convention which the Conservatives had some time ago someone in the hall asked the chairman of the resolutions committee to introduce a resolution stating that family allowances would be increased. That request was refused.
In the avalanche of promises that we heard in two general election campaigns not one word about the matter was spoken by members of the cabinet, the Prime Minister or those who control the party. Not one word was mentioned with regard to increasing family allowances. As a matter of fact there is no legislation on the statute books at the present time nor is there any indication from any speech made or any word spoken which would lead us to hope that there may be an increase in family allowances. But the fact that the Conservatives criticized the family allowance the fact that they have been cold toward it and the fact that there is no legislation on the statute books even today did not stop the Prime Minister or members of his party when in opposition from heaping scorn, criticism, ridicule and abuse on the previous administration for having increased the family allowance by $1. I say, Mr. Chairman, that increasing the family allowance by $1 is one hundred times more than has been done by the present government and one hundred times better than not doing anything at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is $42 million in a full year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is also far more condemnable for the government to sit in cold and stony silence whenever family allowances are mentioned. I wonder what qualification we can give to a political party which, amidst abuse and ridicule, condemns another political party when it has not the courage itself to do even as much. I have certain adjectives which I could use to describe that type of party, Mr. Chairman, but I feel quite sure that I would not be permitted to use them in this house.
Hon. members of the house sitting on the opposite side, including the Solicitor General severely condemned the previous government for increasing the family allowance by only $1 and urged the previous government to increase the family allowance so the children of Canada may be given all the opportunities they deserve. Surely the Solicitor General and hon. members opposite cannot now sit like

Supply-Health and Welfare dummies in their seats. Surely they cannot fail to rise at this time and ask the government to increase family allowances, and condemn it for having ignored family allowances ever since it has been in power. If they do not rise and make speeches of the same type as those they made during the administration of the previous government, Mr. Chairman, what else can we think than that they were not sincere at the time they were making the accusations and at the time they were asking for increases in family allowances?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Where are you going to get the money?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is your problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Another essential requirement of social security legislation which is well founded is the fact that every Canadian who qualifies under the act should receive the benefits of the legislation regardless of religion, race or politics. I am happy to say that all social legislation which is administered by the federal government follows that principle religiously. Anyone who qualifies for any benefit under any type of social legislation administered by the federal government automatically receives it without any condition. But there are other pieces of legislation, and I am thinking in particular of the Old Age Assistance Act and the Disabled Persons Act, to which the federal government contributes in no small measure but which are administered by provincial governments.
I do not know what happens in the other provinces, Mr. Chairman, but I know that in Quebec both these acts have been utilized for political advantage on many occasions by persons who support the present provincial government in the province of Quebec, either as a threat or as an inducement, with respect to people who should normally receive the benefits of the act without any conditions whatsoever being imposed. I suggest that this type of activity is completely intolerable to members of this house. Because of the fact that the federal government contributes more than a little to the cost of this legislation, the government has a responsibility, as has the minister, to see that all people in Canada, including those in the province of Quebec, who qualify for a benefit under social security legislation should receive it without any conditions whatever attached to its receipt. If we do not do that I submit that we are not living in a democracy.
I am also happy, Mr. Chairman, to see that the hospital insurance plan will be coming into effect. I do not think anyone will deny me the right and the pleasure of saying that the previous Liberal administration worked very hard in order to implement a very complicated but very useful scheme. I can also 
say that the previous minister of national health and welfare also contributed greatly to bringing about this insurance scheme. This is not said to take anything away from the present minister. On the contrary, I think he is to be complimented, today being his first anniversary as Minister of National Health and Welfare. I think he has done a wonderful job. I think he deserves a good deal of credit. I sincerely wish him well in the continuation of his mandate as Minister of National Health and Welfare, which we feel will last about three more years. I am happy to see, Mr. Chairman, that as of January 1 British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Newfoundland have already entered into an agreement-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: July 1.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That is right; July 1. I am
happy to see that as of July 1 those provinces have already entered into an agreement with the federal government and that the plan is now operating; and that as of January 1, 1959, Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will likewise participate in the plan. However, I can also say that I am very sorry and I deplore the fact that once again the province of Quebec does not think it wise to enter into such a plan although, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said a while ago, it contributes to funds which are being utilized and from which benefits are being derived in the other provinces of Canada.
I feel very sorry that for reasons better known to himself the premier of the province of Quebec does not see fit to allow the population of Quebec to benefit from this wonderful legislation. Under a Liberal administration, of course, there was no question whatsoever that the province of Quebec might even conceivably come within that act. But with the change of government we are beginning to have a little bit of hope and confidence that Quebec may one day enter into the act. In the London Free Press of May 17, 1958 we read "Quebec Swing Now Seen Toward Hospital Plan". Furthermore, in the Montreal Star of June 7, 1958 there is the headline, "Duplessis Admits Quebec Preparing for Hospital Plan".
May I say that we are very happy indeed that the premier of Quebec should have had such a change of heart, and we are liberal enough to say that we do not care even though the fact that there is a Conservative government at Ottawa, is the reason the premier of Quebec has changed his mind. We are happy, and we hope he will in the very near future communicate with the minister to tell him that he is ready to take part in what I believe to be very beneficial legislation.

I would also urge the minister, because I understand so far he has not done so, to communicate with Premier Duplessis to see if through negotiation it would not be possible to have Quebec join the scheme as soon as possible.
I see that my time has pretty well expired. I may have been rather critical of the Department of National Health and Welfare, but may I say that if this is so I was not being critical of the minister personally or of anyone else in his department. I have brought forward matters about which I feel very strongly, and I hope the minister may be able to give me answers which will help me to understand if perhaps I am wrong.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I would like to compliment the minister on this, the anniversary of his first year in office, and to commend him for the wonderful job he has done. As a member of the medical profession, however, I do feel I should place before him some points of view during this discussion on the estimates of his department.
First, I was quite amazed at the speech made by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, which I think points up the dilemma of the Liberal party. They want to go one way but they have to go the other way, so they end up by stripping their gears. There is no doubt about what he has said in regard to social service in this country in that we have to be able to pay for it, but I think the important thing is for the government to decide on how the distribution of available funds will be effected; and that, of course, is where the former government badly fell down.
In our national Department of National Health and Welfare we have a great number of services having to do with the health of Canadians. The department itself looks after the health of our citizens in the north, the Indians and the Eskimos; it also looks after health matters with respect to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and provides other medical services. The Department of National Defence provides health service for members of our armed forces, and the Department of Veterans Affairs takes care of health service for our veterans. It might be useful if in future our federal departments could get together so as to provide uniform health service to cover those services now provided by the various departments. I think that is important for the future for several reasons; first with respect to civil defence, second
Supply-Health and. Welfare in order to prevent waste of beds and personnel, and third with respect to medical education in Canada.
I will have a little more to say on that aspect of the matter later, but I would like to turn to our hospitalization scheme, which I am sure we are all happy to see put into effect. There are a great many problems to which we must give very serious consideration; and, as the previous speaker said, our social services depend upon the ability of Canada to pay. I think we should immediately recognize that this scheme is going to cost the country a considerable amount of money.
As the hon. member for Timmins pointed out, under this scheme the responsibility for the institution and operation of the service will rest upon the shoulders of the medical profession; I do not think there is any doubt about that. Although I am just a junior member of the profession I personally have no doubt that the medical profession as a whole will be able to accept this responsibility. If, however, we are asking it to accept this responsibility then surely we should give recognition to the profession, at least in the form of an advisory council. In that respect I feel that all parts of the profession should be represented.
Coming now to the hospital scheme itself, I think all members who have gone over the various provincial schemes will agree that with respect to all those provinces which have now entered the agreement or have signified their intention to do so, the main problem is the lack of uniformity as between the provinces in regard to such things as the drugs which are to be provided and the control which will be placed not only on the hospitals but upon the medical profession generally. For example, the arrangement with Saskatchewan contains quite definite restrictions on the drugs which practitioners are allowed to use and which are to be provided under this scheme.
That in itself is not so bad, but what is wrong is that the provincial governments are going to have control and perhaps will act in a deterrent way in respect of the physician practising his profession, in that it will have some say as to the drugs which may or may not be used. That, I can assure the house, is very wrong and very bad for the future of medical care in this country, because as soon as governments at any level become involved in the treatment of patients, then the standard of medical care will deteriorate.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
