speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUSPENSION OF NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated yesterday that a further statement would be made on the question of nuclear tests. Today the President of the United States and the government of the United Kingdom have issued important announcements with regard to their policy in this field.
On behalf of the Canadian government I, and I think all hon. members, welcome unreservedly the decisions which have been reached by the United States and the United Kingdom governments. Indeed, I hope I can speak for all shades of opinion in the house and in the country in welcoming this major development announced this day, and especially to express the satisfaction of members of this house with the statesmanlike and specific nature of the proposals made by those two counfries.
The house will recall that on several occasions since I became Prime Minister I have advocated the suspension of nuclear tests, but always providing there was adequate international control to ensure the observance of the undertakings made in that connection. The principal powers now have before them the result of the technical discussions at Geneva to which Canadian scientists have made an important contribution. These powers are therefore in a favourable position to proceed on a political plane to negotiate the specific terms of an agreement which I hope will be international in effect.
The readiness of the United States and the United Kingdom governments to suspend nuclear tests for a year is a contribution of the first magnitude toward the creation of a favourable atmosphere for negotiation. The conditions that the suspension agreement be extended year by year only if the inspection system is functioning effectively and progress continues to be made in the reaching of

agreements on major substantive disarmament measures, are prudent foundations on which to build. Such understandings will provide a further incentive to creative efforts for the enlargement of mutual confidence and the assurance of the maintenance of peace, and they would emphasize the political significance of an agreement on the suspension of tests as a first step toward disarmament.
It is my profound hope that the Soviet union will shortly indicate its readiness to enter into negotiations for the general purposes set forth in the United States and United Kingdom statements. For our part I can give unqualified assurances that to the extent that the control arrangements which may be agreed upon might be applicable to Canadian territory, we are prepared to co-operate in setting up control stations and inspection of the kind outlined in the report of the experts. Indeed, on more than one occasion Canada has agreed unreservedly to her northern areas and Arctic regions being made available for inspection in order to ensure that surprise attacks will not take place.
At the proper stage of negotiations, which we hope will soon be begun by the powers engaged in active testing programs, the opportunity will come to put forward our detailed views on this matter and to offer constructive suggestions with respect to the location of stations and the administration of inspection teams within Canada.
Sir, after many years of fruitless discussions on the question of disarmament, and indeed the complete breakdown of the machinery of negotiation last year, the world at last has a prospect of agreement in one specific and important field. An agreement for the suspension of nuclear tests would be significant in itself, and might conceivably represent a concrete start on the arduous process of negotiating a disarmament program and agreements which would increase the security of all nations, diminish the danger and fear of war and lighten the burden of armaments.
I trust that in the near future a further round of talks at the expert level will be held on the problem of safeguards and the provision of the necessary means to ensure the maintenance of confidence in this connection.
What has been announced today will give new hope to all mankind. If the U.S.S.R. will now agree to enter into negotiations as suggested in the statements of the United Kingdom and the United States of America, we may this day be entering a new era for the achievement of world peace.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUSPENSION OF NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Perhaps I may be permitted to say a word in regard to the important statement which the Prime Minister has just made. I feel certain that all members of the house will have heard with great satisfaction the decision which has been reached by the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States to suspend nuclear tests for a period of one year. This does, I think, represent one step forward in the effort to bring nuclear weapons of mass destruction under control and, eventually, to abolish them. As such, I am sure we all support the progress which has now been made and which has been mentioned by the Prime Minister.
It remains now, as the Prime Minister has indicated, to work out international arrangements in the United Nations which would confirm and extend the national decisions which have been taken by the United Kingdom, the United States and, previously by the Soviet union. It remains now also to bring this international arrangement which can, I hope, be proceeded with under United Nations control so that public opinion in all countries can be assured that the obligations undertaken in any international arrangement will not be violated. The recent meeting of experts at Geneva which just concluded its work with a positive and constructive report shows that this can be done. It must not be forgotten that a Russian scientist was included in this meeting.
I wish to refer to two paragraphs of that report which certainly have a bearing on what might now be done and I hope will now be done. It is significant to note that these paragraphs were subscribed to by all the scientists there, including the Russian. A newspaper editorial commenting on that portion of the report stated:
The conference of experts reached the conclusion that it is technically feasible to set up, with certain capabilities and limitations, a workable and effective control system for the detection of violations of a possible agreement on the world-wide cessation of nuclear weapons tests.
It was established in this connection that a network of control posts which were equipped with all the necessary apparatus appropriate to the various methods of detection of nuclear explosions should be disposed on continents and on islands, as well as on a few ships in oceans.
I am sure the house will have heard not with surprise but with satisfaction the statement of the Prime Minister that the Canadian government will be happy to co-operate now as it has indicated its willingness to co-operate in the past in any system of control of this kind which requires Canada's co-operation. And so some progress has been achieved, but we must not forget that this is only one step. It is a step taken by nations individually, and it must be made
Supply

Health and Welfare international. There may be difficulties in the way, but I hope those difficulties will be overcome.
The secretary general of the United Nations sent a communication to the conference in Geneva commenting on the report, in which communication was included the following sentence:
It will hereafter lie with the governments concerned and the United Nations to follow through the opening you have created. I have every hope that in due course they will indeed make the necessary constructive effort.
And so, Mr. Speaker, we must all join with the Prime Minister in the hope he has expressed that all nations will follow through in the effort which has begun and which may one day lift this shadow of fear that hangs over the world, the fear that these weapons that could destroy the world might one day be used. Because that fear has been to some extent lessened by what has happened at the Geneva meeting and by the decision announced today in the United Kingdom and the United States, we must rejoice and redouble our own efforts to make further progress.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUSPENSION OF NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without doubt all hon. members of this house and the Canadian people as a whole will be heartened by the good news and the hope engendered by the Prime Minister's statement. As a peace-loving people we respond very quickly to the slightest indication of an improvement in the world situation. I know we all share the wish that the future will justify our hopes in this respect. We trust we may look upon this as a step in the painful progress toward world sanity.
Before concluding I wish to emphasize the fact, particularly on account of the criticism we hear at times of the value of the work of the United Nations, that this present development presents a tremendous opportunity for the United Nations to carry forward the ideas expressed in the Prime Minister's statement.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I was in the process of making some remarks with regard to the national hospitalization scheme and the contracts which have already been entered into. I made the statement that it would be to the detriment of medical care in Canada if

Supply-Health and Welfare government became too involved in such care. I should like to make it quite clear that when I speak of government becoming too involved in matters of this kind I mean in terms of interference in the doctor-patient relationship.
There is no doubt that government has a very real responsibility with regard to hospitalization, and that has been shown by the introduction of the national hospitalization act. However, I feel that perhaps the government and the house have not given sufficient consideration to just what this act will entail and what responsibility we will have under the act. When I first came to Ottawa I was surprised to learn that there is not a standing committee of this house concerning national health and welfare. That is an omission which should be rectified in the near future in my opinion, having regard to the amount of money that is going to be spent by this department. In that connection I should like to point out to the committee some of the questions we will have to consider if we are going to make the scheme work as economically as possible.
First and foremost, of course, is the question of hospital beds. There is a shortage of hospital beds at this time, particularly in certain areas. It is not only a matter of making more beds available, but we must derive the best use possible from the beds we do have. Some of the previous speakers have noted that we have to assure that active treatment hospital beds are kept available for people requiring active treatment. We have a responsibility to see that our older people are provided accommodation so they may be released from hospital. We have an equal responsibility to ensure that veterans are cared for without having to remain in active treatment hospitals occupying essential hospital beds.
A second consideration in the responsibility of accommodation is that of making sure we supply the most modern equipment that is available, and make it available to all the people in Canada. I hope this will be taken care of.
The next big responsibility which the federal government has and to which we should be giving serious consideration is the matter of personnel to man the massive hospitalization program and to assure that the Canadian people are getting their money's worth from this expenditure. In that connection we must make sure that Canada maintains her present position in the field of medical education, post-graduate education and interne education. I wish to draw to the attention of hon. members of the committee that interne education is an important field. We are losing a great many internes,


particularly to the United States, for various reasons. Certainly one reason is that they do not receive the necessary remuneration to permit them to remain in Canada. Governments all across Canada are spending vast sums of money subsidizing the education of internes at universities, but we must not stop there. We must assist them to continue to study in Canada and practise here.
There is also the problem of the shortage of nurses. As the hospitalization scheme is implemented across Canada the number of nurses required will be greatly increased. As hon. members know, there is a definite shortage at this time. I think the plea of the hon. member for Athabasca, made in the house some time ago, in regard to the federal government giving consideration to paying a subsidy to nurses, should be acted upon, and I would certainly commend it to the minister for his consideration.
Then there are the other personnel who in this modern day and age have charge of facilities in the hospitals. I refer to the various technicians in the laboratories, X-ray rooms, and so on. We have to take the lead in the education of those people. We have to do it now; we have to supply opportunities to be educated in Canada; we have to make sure that they are properly looked after when they graduate, so they will stay in Canada and help us in this job of hospitalization.
Because this hospitalization scheme is of such national importance and because, as I said previously, the responsibility for its efficient working is going to rest on the shoulders of the medical profession, I believe they should have some help in that regard. I believe the Department of National Health and Welfare has a responsibility to educate the boys and girls in our schools. They should make more material available than has been made available up to now. I commend the department for the books that have been put out, particularly the books on child care and more particularly on the book "Canadian Mother and Child", and also other books that have been put out over the years. They are excellent books. I think more could be done for the junior age group in our high schools. More literature should be available to them, because there is no doubt that an educated public is going to be required to make this hospitalization scheme work.
We can go on from there as far as education is concerned, but certainly the federal government has a serious responsibility in one regard. I refer to medical research. In the past, of course, we have had the Connaught laboratories, but it is going to be more important in the future in cancer research and all other medical research which have to be

undertaken. I am sure the minister is quite aware of this, but I just mention it to bring it to his attention again.
There is just one other problem that I should like to bring to the attention of the committee at this time, namely the problem of the general practitioner in Canada. I feel that something should be done in this regard, because I feel very strongly that the general practitioner is the backbone of the medical service in Canada and will be the backbone of the hospitalization scheme if it is to work. It is vitally important that we do not relegate the general practitioner to the status of a file clerk, because if we do that the whole scheme will break down.
One other thing I should like to say in that regard has to do with civil defence. Probably most hon. members are aware that if-and I say "if"; from the announcement we just heard it becomes a little more remote-we are ever involved in a nuclear war our major medical centres would in all probability be involved in that war and would be of no use to us. We must keep in mind that the backbone of our civil defence in so far as the medical corps is concerned will be the country hospitals in rural areas and our general practitioners in those areas. If we are to make sure that we have the buildings and the people ready to take over that responsibility, then we have to guard very jealously the position of the general practitioner. I am happy to say that in Canada the general practitioners are very fortunate in that so far their position has been recognized.
If I may, I would like to say one other word in regard to the senior citizens of this country, our older people, our pioneers, and their housing accommodation. This has always been a very great problem in all communities in Canada, in that we have always had the problem of looking after our older citizens. Many governments have the idea that all they have to do is build some sort of marble hall and stick those people in there and forget about them. Many of our provincial governments are doing that right now. They are building 400-bed homes for the chronic aged in the cities.
I can tell the committee-and I am sure most hon. members will agree with me-that our old people do not want to go into those marble halls. They want to have some accommodation, yes, but they want to have that accommodation and maintain their independence, because after all they are Canadians. I am a little disappointed that some of the provinces of Canada have not taken advantage of the help which is available under the present legislation through Central Mortgage and Housing to provide the type
Supply-Health and Welfare of accommodation which our old people want and need. I trust we are not going to keep on building huge marble halls in cities or in other areas. Those people want to stay at home with their friends; they want to have some independence.
In conclusion I should like to commend the minister on his work in the past year. My remarks with regard to the hospitalization scheme I would like to be taken as concerning something which will happen and which we are going to have to take into consideration and fulfil as the rest of Canada becomes involved in the scheme.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which is of concern to my constituency, and it is no doubt a condition which obtains in every other constituency in the country. I wish to speak briefly on pensions in relation to health. Under the present legislation an old age pension is not payable without a means test until a person has reached the age of 70, when he or she, by the way, is subject to failing health.
As everyone knows, in most industries now the normal retiring age is 65, and in most instances the employees are retired with no pension or with a very small pension. During the period 65 to 70 most citizens still have to meet fixed commitments such as mortgage or rental payments, which are proving increasingly more difficult with the reduced value of the dollar owing to rising costs; call it inflation, if you like. The fact remains that what was once considered a small pension has now shrunk to a totally inadequate and ridiculously low level, and is certainly not sufficient to meet doctors' bills.
Legislation should be introduced to eliminate the means test at 65. I should like to read a paragraph or two from a letter which I received from one of my constituents, which tells part of the story:
I am a retired C.N.R. man, having been off now for over three years. I have, up until now, been fortunate enough to find work for part of the year but lately I have been unable to secure work.
I thought I had a job lined up with the department of highways at Fort William but I now find I am too old. I want it understood that I have no complaint with the officials of the department of highways. They were very courteous and took my application but later informed me they had instructions not to hire anyone over 65 years of age. That in itself I think is all right as there are many younger people who cannot find jobs.
It is one of the tragedies of our times that retired men and women, most of whom devoted their lives to the public service, are now caught in a vicious cost-price squeeze. Twenty years ago a man could look forward to a fairly comfortable retirement on a few thousand dollars or on a guaranteed pension of say $25 or $30 per month. These people
3948	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare are now living on the ragged edge of abject poverty, and that is a condition which should not be tolerated in this great and wealthy country of Canada. Surely it is not too much to ask that pensions of civil servants, who have to pay for medical services, for instance, be brought under review and increased to the point where retirement after a lifetime of service means a peaceful rest from labour and worry.
I am aware that this particular matter was thoroughly discussed on Monday, December 16, 1957, as reported in Hansard, but unfortunately the resolution under discussion at that time was talked out. That resolution had been introduced by my predecessor, Rev. Dan Mclvor. I have practically the same resolution on the order paper, but unfortunately it will go into oblivion so far as the present session of the house is concerned. This resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to increase the pension of civil servants and Royal Canadian Mounted Police who were retired after long service when salaries were low, so as to bring their pensions in line with those of the present.
The question of pensions is one which should be considered and which should be under constant review in order to prevent the inequalities which now exist in so far as our retired civil servants and members of the R.C.M.P. are concerned. There are other categories, of course, which should receive consideration, not the least of which are the widows and unmarried women. These categories should receive pensions at the age of 60, and the reasons for that are obvious. Everyone knows that a single woman at the age of 60 cannot easily obtain employment, and unless she has independent means she is left to the mercy of charity or cast on the relief rolls of the municipality in which she lives.
I should like also to commend the hon. member for Carleton, who was in the house a few moments ago but is now out of the chamber, for the very creditable presentation he made last December on this question as reported in Hansard. I express the hope that his views on the matter have not changed since he made this statement:
I say the government is not acting justly toward retired civil servants in not granting an increase in their superannuation.
The government has given an indication that they will consider this aspect of the situation, and it is to be hoped that they will do something about it soon.
All persons who require hospitalization, Mr. Chairman, will be taken care of under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services [Mr. Badania.l

Act, with the exception of those who are placed in nursing homes. They must bear this expense, and if the patient is an indigent such cost must be borne by the municipality. I say that today municipalities are charged with costs of all descriptions as a result of many demands made upon them, to which the provinces and the federal government do not contribute what I would consider to be a fair share. I believe some provision should be made in this health insurance measure to include nursing home care. I would appreciate it very much if the minister would give assurance that nursing home care will be included within the scope of this measure.
I do not want to make a lengthy speech. I realize there are many others who want to speak on this subject, and for that reason I shall make these remarks very brief indeed. However, I want to express my deep appreciation for the consideration which the department has given certain cases that have come within my knowledge. I sincerely trust the department will continue to give the maximum assurance to the people of Canada that their welfare is going to be taken care of, and that welfare benefits will be increased to meet conditions as they exist at this time.
We are moving quickly into a new era. What was good three or four years ago is no longer good. Some people are apt to condemn the former government for many omissions, but I do not believe such criticism is justified because what they did a few years ago perhaps met the conditions at that time. We are living now in a different time altogether. What we are doing today will not be good enough next year or five or ten years from now. I maintain, therefore, that we should keep these conditions under constant review.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The matter which I should
like to discuss for just a few minutes at this stage, Mr. Chairman, is civil defence. I am sure that all of us heard with satisfaction the statement made a few minutes ago by the Prime Minister to the effect that an agreement has been reached between the United States and the United Kingdom to suspend nuclear tests for one year. I know the details of this agreement have not yet been worked out and the precise control arrangements have not yet been completed; but, as the Prime Minister said and as the Leader of the Opposition repeated, this is probably the first significant step which has been made in recent years toward disarmament.
If we are successful in keeping the peace the measures which might be undertaken here to equip ourselves to try to withstand a nuclear war will not be necessary. But so long as the threat of such a catastrophe

hangs over the world it behooves us to take every intelligent step we can to ensure that as far as possible we are protecting our people from the awful consequences of a nuclear attack.
I should like to commend the Minister of National Health and Welfare for the very clear and helpful statement he made when introducing his estimates this afternoon. I should also like to congratulate him not only on the hard work he has put into the affairs of that department over the past year, but also on the excellent manner in which he has described the activities of his department to people in many communities of Canada. In the last day or two I had the opportunity of reading several speeches made by that hon. gentleman to community groups. I believe he is fulfilling in an admirable way the obligation he has to inform the Canadian public as to the important welfare activities of his department.
Just as there is no such thing as an adequate program of military preparedness, as was pointed out earlier by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, so there can be no really adequate program carried out in the field of civil defence. According to the estimates before us some $7 million are proposed to be appropriated for this purpose. On the other hand, some $1,680 million are to be used in equipping this country either to defend itself from attack or to retaliate against a power which may attack this country.
I am not going to suggest that there should be any ratio or relationship between money appropriated for defence purposes and money appropriated for civil defence purposes. Nor am I going to say that in view of this serious menace that confronts the world we should spend huge sums of money to provide shelter facilities and other means of protecting ourselves against the effects of a nuclear war.
What I do say, however, Mr. Chairman, is that this matter of civil defence is a national responsibility. It is the responsibility of the parliament of Canada. I realize that the work to be carried out in this field cannot be carried out exclusively by the national government. Some aspects of it, of course, must be delegated to the provincial authorities and the municipal governments. But what I do say is this. The time has come in this country for us to get down to the serious business of establishing a positive, definite and intelligent policy in this field. I must say that at the moment we have nothing of this kind. I realize that the minister, under whose jurisdiction this matter falls, has been fully occupied with work in other important fields. However, I hope 57071-3-250
Supply-Health and Welfare that within a very few weeks' time he can direct his attention and that of the officials of his department in a serious way to this matter.
As I understand it, the duties of the civil defence co-ordinator are threefold. He has the duty first of all to co-ordinate federal planning and action; second, to co-ordinate and advise provincial and municipal authorities; and third to maintain liaison with corresponding agencies in the United Kingdom, the United States and other countries. Those are the broad and general spheres of his authority. Of course they will mean very little so far as the Canadian people are concerned unless something is done to implement them.
It seems to me that very little money is required to do the basic things that must be done in this field, and I think they should be done soon. First of all I think there is required to be set up and well publicized by the national government of this country an adequate warning system. I venture to say, Mr. Chairman, that you could go out into the streets of Ottawa today and talk to the first 100 people you met and ask each of them what kind of warning he would expect to have should there be an attack of Russian jet bombers over this country, and you would not get a very satisfactory answer from anyone. I say this thing can be done rather simply, without the expenditure of a great deal of money, and that it is simply foolish to have different kinds of warning systems coming into being in the different municipalities across the country.
The second thing I think should be done right away in this matter, Mr. Chairman, is that the national authorities should make available to the people advice as to the simple activities they should undertake in the event that there is warning of such an attack. The other day I had the experience of going to the civil defence headquarters of this nation not many hundred yards away from this chamber. I went there at the request of an eminent Toronto architect who desired that I seek information with respect to the construction of a shelter under a private dwelling. I was told that the authorities really had not made up their minds as to what to recommend in this field. After a long time there was finally produced to me a single sheet of paper on which was sketched in very rough form a proposed shelter which had some kind of approval of the government of Canada. But when one sought to find out just what kind of approval this was, the answer was very evasive indeed.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that it is simply disgraceful that at this time a citizen can go

Supply-Health and Welfare to the civil defence authorities of Canada and be told that they have really no positive recommendations to make with respect to the kind of shelter one might build under his dwelling house so he might have some kind of chance of surviving an attack of the kind I have mentioned.
The other very few proposals I have in this matter, Mr. Chairman, are simple. It seems to me that the national government should undertake, with the assistance of well-qualified traffic engineers, rather extensive studies to work out the method by which people are to be evacuated from large centres of population. I also believe it would not be a costly thing to set up short training schools, of say two or three days' duration, for people who desire to learn the basic things necessary in order to conduct themselves in an intelligent way in their communities should war occur. I think training of this kind could be given at such places as county fairs, the central Canadian exhibition and the Canadian national exhibition. I believe people across the country would enrol in large numbers if they knew that by taking six, eight or ten hours of training they would gain the basic information which they need in order to do the best that could be done under the circumstances for themselves and their families should war break out.
Finally, I think the government should consider making use of the pilots of this country. I know they are prepared to cooperate with the Department of National Defence and the Department of National Health and Welfare by equipping themselves to assist the civilian population if necessary. I also know that in the United States there are some 80,000 civilian airmen enrolled in a voluntary organization, and that much has been done in this field.
Such pilots could be very useful indeed in the locating of areas of serious damage and in transporting medical and food supplies to isolated communities in the event of war. I am confident that if an approach were made to the flying clubs' association and to the Canadian owners' and pilots' association much could be done in this regard without the spending of very much money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext:
I would like to say a few words in connection with three items covered by the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and I should like to deal first with the hospital insurance plan. I understand that this plan is now in operation in two provinces, namely in Alberta and British Columbia, and that from January 1 next it will operate in the province of Ontario. I also understand that supplementary estimates will be brought forward

from time to time in order to cover the cost of the federal share of this plan.
I wish to remind the minister that Canadians as a whole are contributing to the operation of such plan and, speaking now as the representative of a Quebec riding, I would point out to the minister and his government how disturbed and disappointed we are at the prospect of paying for this plan yet not benefiting from it in our own province. We all know that the premier of Quebec must be blamed for the negative stand taken on this issue, but I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare is in the same boat, in view of his lack of imagination and initiative and for not having at least taken one step to induce or invite the authorities of Quebec to join in the plan.
To illustrate my point I wish to refer specifically to page 1432 of Hansard for June 19, 1958, where the hon. member for St. Denis asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare the following question:
-does the minister not think that the premier of Quebec is rather late in trying to take advantage of this wonderful legislation?
The minister replied:
I do not think it is for me to say what I think. All I can announce is that there has been no indication from the province of Quebec as to what their intentions may be.
The member for St. Denis then asked the following supplementary question:
There was no letter, no telephone call, no correspondence between the premier of Quebec and the federal government?
To which the minister replied:
No indication.
Next I would like to refer to page 3861 of Hansard for August 21, where I am recorded as having asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare the following question: Would the minister tell us if he has received recently an indication from the government of the province of Quebec as to their intention to join in the hospitalization insurance scheme?
The minister replied as follows:
No, Mr. Speaker.
Whereupon I asked him the following supplementary question:
Would the minister tell us if he has lately contacted the authorities of the province of Quebec, whether by telephone or telegram to that effect?
To which the minister replied:
No, Mr. Speaker.
The admission by the minister that he has not even written, phoned or sent a telegram to the Quebec government inviting it to join in this plan is, in my view and in the view of most members on this side of the house, one of the most amazing features of this

session. Does the minister believe that the citizens of the province of Quebec will willingly pay by way of taxes for a plan which is going to benefit all provinces except Quebec? I say now, and I think this is a principle which the minister cannot challenge, that this is a national plan which must operate on a national scale. Here again we can measure the tremendous need for a federal-provincial conference and the failure of this government to call such a conference as promised. This, in my view, is the reason the citizens of the province of Quebec will once again be the object of discrimination on the part of this government.
If the premier of the province of Quebec until now has refused to enter this plan he has a reason, and it is up to the minister to inquire as to that reason and find a formula to suit the exigencies of Mr. Duplessis, whatever they might be. If the minister is too shy to discuss the matter with Mr. Duplessis, why does he not ask the Prime Minister to pinch hit for him? The premier of Quebec and the Prime Minister are two good friends; they share the same views on many problems of the day, and they are using the same approach to many political issues.
We hope something will be done next session. We do hope that we will not have the same negative answers from the minister and that the minister will not deal with this issue as he has done so far. This is one of the first matters into which we are going to inquire at the opening of the next session. (Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I have something to say about family allowances. The country will always be grateful to the Liberal administration for having introduced them, and everyone will recall that the former leader of the Conservative party, Mr. Drew, had fought against them tooth and nail. However we did introduce them, and they are now on the statute books. Since 1945, various amendments have increased the amounts, and in the budget speech of 1957 the amount was set at $6 per month for children under 10, and $8 per month for children aged 10 to 16.
It is fitting to recall that at that time, in 1957, the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) criticized us because he claimed that the family allowances in 1957 did not have the same purchasing power as in 1945. May I say also that if, as we were told by the Solicitor General, family allowances were to have gone up in 1957, there is all the more reason they should go up now, considering the marked rise in the cost of living since June 1957, as evidenced by the following figures, obtained from the bureau of statistics, relating to basic family necessities:

Before ending my remarks I should like to say a few words concerning civil defence. Previous speakers on both sides have touched on this important question and in view of the announcement made by the Prime Minister yesterday that in the case of emergency there would be a plan based on the decentralization of government in this country, and in the light of the present international situation, I think this problem is more acute today than it has ever been in the past.

Supply-Health and Welfare
I remember very well that when the Conservative members were sitting on this side of the house they pressed us strongly for action with regard to civil defence. When we were responsible for the administration we made what we thought was a good start, but I remember that the present Postmaster General was on his feet on several occasions asking the government what they were planning to do for the city of Montreal in case of nuclear war. I do not want to go into detail here, because the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has covered the ground pretty well, but I say to the minister that if those contentions were true in 1957 they are even more true today. What we need in a city such as Montreal, which is on an island, is a third bridge in case a quick evacuation should be required. It is my intention to bring this matter up during discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Transport, but I wondered when I was listening to the remarks of some of the previous speakers if we should not put this item of civil defence under the Department of National Defence. Both subjects are close together, and should war break out we would all be in the front line.
Anyway, these are suggestions which I make in very good faith and in no way to embarrass the minister or the government. I hope the minister will be good enough to make a few comments on them when we reach the end of his estimates.

Mr. Chairman, when the debate began this morning I was more or less intrigued with the remarks of the hon. member for Timmins, likewise with those of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres and the other contributions which have been made, since these followed the same technique and pattern as was followed after we returned in 1957.
In June, 1957, the C.C.F. line of approach was that we had not done it soon enough, and the opposition at that time, the Liberals, said that we did not go far enough. The hon. member for Timmins spent considerable time this morning in repeating excerpts from speeches that were made by the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet and other hon. members of the government when they were in opposition. I would say that there is no intention to retract or retrace our steps from that particular time when we were advocating that certain things should take place.
I am speaking, now, with regard to the hospitalization bill which had been brought in by the previous minister of national health and welfare. We did, undoubtedly, advocate that certain advances should take place with

regard to that particular policy, but when you start to make a resume of what has taken place prior to that you find that the policy of the Liberal party had been such that they had promised the people of Canada from 1919 onward that they were going to introduce a hospital scheme for this country, and election after election they had dished it up to the people that this was going to take place. But the promise was never fulfilled, and even with respect to the program they turned out for the 1919 election it turned out it was only a program formed on the basis of political expediency.
What had really taken place, of course, was that the people of Canada and particularly the people of the province of Ontario had become so fed up with the diet of empty excuses that had been dished out to them for years by the previous Liberal administration that they took the matter in hand. The people were faced with mounting bills for hospitalization. This imposed a heavy burden on them which they simply could not meet. The hospitals in the province of Ontario took it upon themselves to initiate a program under which the people of that province could prepay hospital bills. The idea was welcomed by the people of the province and over 49 per cent of the population subscribed to one program or another through which they could prepay hospital bills. The concept grew in popularity until a need was created for additional hospitals in the province. The demand for additional hospitals and the number of people seeking treatment reached such gigantic proportions that the province decided to take the situation in hand and do something about it. The situation was studied for two of three years and the province come up with a program which it was planned to have inaugurated in that province. They were required to do this on account of the dilatory and lackadaisical attitude on the part of the government of Mackenzie King and Mr. St. Laurent in approaching the problem.

This was brought in because of conditions in the province of Ontario. It does not matter who brought it in. The people of Ontario determined the situation because so many of them had subscribed to Blue Cross and the Ontario hospitalization and physicians' program that it created a need for the construction of additional hospitals. The time came when it could be avoided no longer. The premier of Ontario announced that he would introduce a hospitalization scheme of his own. The previous Liberal administration had to act smartly in order to bring in a scheme to counteract it. Those are the circumstances surrounding the introduction of the hospitalization bill by the previous government.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are now saying that this government has not gone far enough or fast enough. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is to be complimented on the fact that he has undertaken to put this scheme into effect. It is quite true that we have not included tuberculosis sanatoria, hospitals for the mentally ill nor have we provided for depreciation of hospitals, but a great step forward has been taken. And let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that the Diefenbaker government inaugurated the things promised by the Prime Minister. We have not yet gone all the way but we are making progress. The Prime Minister has
Supply-Health and Welfare inaugurated many of the measures he promised to institute and has succeeded in instilling in the minds and hearts of the Canadian people a full measure of confidence in him and his government. The Canadian people feel that in their Prime Minister they have a man who is worthy of their confidence and who will do something for them. They know he will fulfil promise after promise and unlike his predecessors in office of the Liberal party he will not hold out empty promises. He has already made a splendid start toward implementing many of the programs to which he referred during the election campaign.
But hon. gentlemen opposite have tried to frustrate him. They opposed and balked him at every turn from October 1957 to January 1, 1958, until he said, "Let us go to the people and we shall see who they want". And so he went to the country and the people made their choice on March 31. The Prime Minister won their full confidence again. My hon. friends opposite say the Canadian people have no confidence or faith in the Prime Minister. He went to the people on March 31 this year and the people gave him their answer. He was returned with the largest majority there has ever been in this house.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

I shall accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I was merely following the line of argument advanced this morning by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres in which he made the statement that the people of this country did not believe in the program being offered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He dealt with the question of old age pensions in his remarks and said we have gone too far, that the previous government had considered it unsound to increase pensions following an examination of the financial basis of the question. Like my good friend the hon. member for Cochrane did a moment ago in trying to distract me from the line of argument I was presenting, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres sought to obscure the issue and brought up the question of family allowances and said we had not done enough in that respect. But in the 1953 election we remember that the

Supply

Health and Welfare Liberals said our senior citizens had not been too well looked after but after four years the Liberal government failed to take action and still had done nothing for them. The situation pyramided because of the increased cost of living to the point where the people could stand it no longer.
The present government listened to the pleas of the people and gave them the increase they deserved and required. The previous administration offered them an insultingly paltry amount that did not begin to meet their needs. This government gave the people what they wanted with regard to old age pensions and that is why the present government is in office. The hon. member for Jasper-Edson commented on the fluctuating policy of the Liberals. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres said they were following the right course. Yes, they followed the right course; the course that was the perfect one to result in their being relegated to sit on that side of the house. They are sitting where they are now because of the course they followed.
The present government increased old age pensions to an extent that enabled recipients of old age pensions to live in dignity. The Prime Minister promised that the pension would be increased from time to time as the requirement arose. Hon. gentlemen opposite can argue from now until doomsday about whether or not the people of Canada are satisfied with the performance of this government but they will be wasting their time because the Canadian people have absolute confidence in their Prime Minister and his government. The previous administration was so convinced of its own infallibility that it felt it was permanently entrenched on the government benches and could impose any policy it cared to on the Canadian people. That government failed to give the people what they wanted with respect to health and welfare.

Very well, Mr. Chairman. I believe I have covered the ground sufficiently in order to prove to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres and the hon. member for Cochrane that the program inaugurated by this government perfectly satisfies the Canadian people. I must admit I really had no intention of speaking at this time but

their remarks got me so worked up that I felt I had to rise and put them in their place.
I am perfectly satisfied with what has been done by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and I am convinced he will do the right thing for the people in this country with respect to hospitalization and the other things hon. members are worrying about. I would tell them that they can trust to the honesty, fidelity and political sincerity of the Prime Minister of this country to ensure that the people will get what they require and everything they were promised. All promises will be lived up to.
I have taken a great personal interest in the question of civil defence to which reference was made by the hon. member for York Centre. In this field too the blame can be laid on the doorstep of the previous government which failed to take action. We now have a government that has taken the matter in hand. An investigation is being conducted concerning whether civil defence should be under civil authority or under the militia. What will be the result? You will find that it will be the same course and the same procedure that has been followed ever since the present Prime Minister took office, who will decide on the right policy for the people at the right time and give it to them as they want it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to tell the minister that anything I may say today will not be directed at him personally. It is something I have to say, and I hope he will understand because if I had a wish to make it is that he remain the Minister of National Health and Welfare for the duration of the time of this government. Of course, after that it will be his affair to get elected, but if he gets elected I hope he will sit on this side of the house.
On May 20 of this year I made a speech in this house calling the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to the serious inroads the drug habit was making on the youth of Canada. I also stated, based on police evidence submitted to me, the rapid spread noted in the use of goofballs, the first step to drug addiction among teenagers. Based on facts, as I have said, I asked in this house that the drugs in goofballs be placed under the narcotics act so as to facilitate the arrest and conviction of the drug pushers in order that our youth may be protected against the drug evil.
Following my speech in this house, a certain gentleman by the name of H. R. Hart, an official of the Department of National Health and Welfare, evidently gave an interview to

a reporter of the Montreal Star, which interview appeared in that newspaper under date of Saturday, May 24, 1958. In this interview he stated that there was no goofball problem and therefore the statements that I had made in this house were not true. I believe this man Hart is an old employee of the department and, as such, he should have known that it is not proper for a menial employee of the department to give interviews to newspapers, thereby ignoring his minister who is supposed to answer for his department in this house.
Why this employee was so anxious to deny my statements I cannot understand. The facts I have placed on the record so far would seem to more than justify any statements I made and to show that Hart did not know what he was talking about. Hart not only denied what I had said in good faith in this house, based on sound facts, but he deliberately slandered a group of professional gentlemen without any basis whatever for his accusations. I would say that he is a very unreliable official, and he is also a dangerous man; for although he has deliberately slandered an outstanding group of professional men he has done nothing to repair the damage he did. I refer to the druggists of Outremont.
I hold in my hand, Mr. Chairman, a copy of the July, 1958, issue of "Prevention", the official organ in the province of Quebec of the Quebec police and fire chiefs' association. On page 58 of this issue appears the following article in French concerning what "Prevention" called: "Un Mai Social", meaning in English "a social evil". In other words, they consider goofballs a social evil. I am sorry this is in French. There is no English version therefore I will have to read it in French.
(Translation):

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
In an attempt to ward off a social evil which is preying on the adolescents of the province of Quebec, the federal Department of National Health and Welfare is calling upon all druggists to put an end to the sale of drug substitutes.
Last week-end alone, the R.C.M.P. received more than twenty complaints concerning adolescents who had taken those tranquillizers or barbiturates popularly known as "goofballs".
Similar representations have been received from people in several parts of the province, including several quarters in the Montreal area. Some of the representations have been made by parents who are concerned over the present conditions and the possible fate of their children if they become goofball addicts. Representations have also been made by various police departments.
It has been established beyond doubt that youngsters are getting into the habit of taking goofballs in such youth centres as colleges, high schools, recreation rooms and dance halls.
Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
An official spokesman of the Social Welfare Court told us: "This evil seems to be taking on increasingly alarming proportions. It seems to have started among our adolescents three years ago, along with the advent of 'leatherjackets'
With an eye on this social evil which plagues the physical and moral health of youngsters, the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare instituted judicial proceedings several weeks ago against 25 Montreal druggists who sold tranquillizers to adolescents without prescriptions. Similar proceedings were instituted against druggists in Quebec, Shawinigan, Grand-Mere, Three Rivers, Valleyfield and other parts of the province. All defendants were found guilty and sentenced to pay a fine.
The authorities take the most serious view of goofball addiction, because, with the black market in drugs at its lowest level for some years past, addicts can take goofballs as a substitute for drugs.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Only a few days ago, two guards at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary were dismissed for having brought in goofballs for prisoners.
An inquiry was recently held in Bordeaux prison, where goofballs had been brought in at the time of arrival of two prisoners charged with hold-up. One of the men had been arrested by the detectives of the Hold-Up Squad of the Montreal Police Department, and at the time of his arrest, Detective Captain Joseph Bedard noted that the two accused "were in a total drug stupor when they were taken into custody-and were just about to rob a bank".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
We are informed by the authorities that, in some areas, the number of teenagers using goofballs has gone up from 40 per cent to 250 per cent in three years.
Inspector Ovila Pelletier, chief of the Youth Welfare squad of the Montreal police, informed us that the matter is the most serious problem he has to cope with at this time. As an example he stated that last week-end a 20-year old girl was taken to Misericordia Hospital in a very critical condition after taking an overdose of goofballs at a teenage party.
The judicial proceedings taken against some druggists by the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare have brought praise from several social groups, authorities of the Social Welfare Court, young people's associations and other groups, in view of the very serious view they take of the problem.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. Joseph Portius, special prosecutor in the matter for the federal Department of National Health and Welfare, stated: "We are finding it very difficult to apply the law, and if druggists do not observe the law more closely, a scourge will soon be upon us".
Mr. Joseph Saint-Onge, of the Department of National Health and Welfare, informs us that the government and the College of Pharmacy have advised all druggists of the problem, and reminded them that it is illegal to sell goofballs without a doctor's prescription.
Offenders can be fined from $500 to $5,000, and be sentenced to a prison term of three to six months.
Habitual use of goofballs by youngsters seeking new thrills can seriously harm their health, upset their nervous and digestive systems, and can even result in death.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Supply-Health and Welfare
Like narcotics, these capsules, which cost only three to six cents on the open market, fetch a much higher price on the black market.
Thus some of the drug pushers sell them at a dollar a piece.

As I said previously, Mr. Chairman, I have just quoted from the official organ of the Quebec police and fire chiefs' association.
I have previously placed on the record a news item published in Time, the Canadian edition of March 31, 1958, entitled "Nova Scotia Goofball Crackdown". It is stated therein that a young school boy, 14 years of age, had died after absorbing goofballs. I also placed on the record another article published in the Montreal Star of March 25, 1958, under the heading "Goofballs Smuggled into Prison". On this occasion a serious mutiny occurred in the jail as a result of goofballs, causing serious and costly damage. I believe I have established that if Chief H. R. Hart of the inspection services of the Department of National Health and Welfare does not know a goofball problem exists, then it is high time he woke up. We are experiencing here a modern version of Rome burning while Nero fiddles. We have a most serious goofball problem in Canada and yet he, the chief, does not know it exists. The Montreal Star stated as follows in its edition of Saturday, May 24, 1958:
Mr. Hart conceded that there have been prosecutions of pharmacists in Outremont for illegal sales of medicinals which can only be sold on prescription, and that $100 fines were imposed, in spite of requests from the federal Department of National Health and Welfare for stiffer penalties.
This, Mr. Chairman, I absolutely deny. It is an outright lie and an unwarranted slander on the druggists of Outremont. As mayor of the city of Outremont, I am proud to be able to state in this house that never, and I repeat "never", has a druggist of the city of Outremont been arrested, brought to court or condemned for having infringed the drug act in any way. Outremont possesses the finest group of ethical druggists on the North American continent. Whatever Hart said about the Outremont druggists was, as I stated previously, an absolute lie. He deliberately slandered these professional gentlemen, and I should like to know what the minister intends to do about repairing the unwarranted damage that has been done to the reputation of these outstanding ethical druggists by the irresponsible official that Hart is.
