speechtext:
Owing to my position in the house over a period of 13 years, Mr. Chairman, when the estimates of this department


were under consideration I used to face certain esteemed senior officials of the department. I must express my pleasure at having the opportunity, for the first time, to gaze upon the more attractive features of this department.
I want to again briefly urge the government to consider the early establishment of a complete national health insurance plan. I am not going to repeat the arguments made by previous speakers in this group today and on previous occasions. I just want to emphasize my interest in this matter and the interest of a large number of Canadians. In that connection, before passing on, I want to quote from today's Gazette in which there appears a little article entitled, "N.H.S. A Way of Life".
London, July 11-
Critics of the cradle-to-the-grave health service claim that far from being "free", it is costing plenty in taxes.
But surveys show that the man-in-the-street is solidly behind the plan.
I d rather pay as I go than run the risk of going broke over medical fees," is the typical reaction.
The national health service covers anything from psychiatric treatment to nose-straightening if it is recommended by a doctor.
The criterion is not "what can this patient afford?" but "what would be best for him?"
It is in that respect I want to emphasize my attitude towards this very important question. I do hope that in an early session of parliament we will see some response from the government to this demand for a complete national health insurance scheme.
Before proceeding, I also want to express my support for the representations made by this group and other members who have spoken today for further consideration of the needs of persons who have not reached 70 years of age to qualify for old age security as a matter of right. We have a long way to go in that direction. We have made some advances in recent years. A wealthy country like this can do better than it is doing at the moment to meet the needs and requirements of a large section of the elderly population. I refer to women from 60 to 70 and men from 65 to 70, who are not cared for properly under the present circumstances.
Having said that, and before proceeding, I do want to take this opportunity to express my appreciation of the importance of this department and the excellent work being done by the staff in Ottawa and throughout the country. I have had the opportunity of talking to civil servants and other senior persons from Great Britain who are interested in problems of national health and welfare

I hear nothing but admiration expressed tor the officials of this department. I think we in Canada, generally speaking, have a right to be proud of our civil servants and I say that without any hesitation. I say it as a result of some 13 years experience in this house, which experience provided me with an opportunity to meet a good number of these people.
Having said that, I must say I was pondering this morning how, in order not to be repetitious as accused by the Globe and Mail or unnecessarily taking up the time of the house, I could do the greatest good for the greatest number in the shortest possible time during this debate. I have come to the conclusion that possibly I could do most in the few minutes I wish to take by saying that a good many people in Canada, I judge from the inquiries I have received, want to know the truth about royal queen bee jelly.
I find that this royal queen bee jelly is advertised in numerous periodicals across Canada and the United States. I have seen advertisements recommending it as a cosmetic. In fact, I met a lady today who uses it frequently and who says it is very good in that respect. I have met others who do not believe in it. I have seen it advertised as a skin food. I have seen it advertised as an antiseptic for open wounds. I have seen it advertised as a rejuvenator for old people. I find here in the Ottawa Citizen of August 20, 1958 the following:
Queen bee royal jelly capsules and royal jelly creme for wrinkles, loose and rough skin,-
That would not apply to me.
-now available Thuna Herbalist, 397 Bank, CE-2-6388.
Tlie same advertisement is repeated in the Journal. Strangely enough, while I have made a search of the papers I can only find this type of advertisement with respect to royal jelly in the eastern periodicals and papers. Apparently it is not thought so necessary or required in western Canada. In any event, that has just been the result of my research to date. I have not with me at the present time one of the advertisements but I saw one in a United States paper advertising this royal queen bee jelly as an antiseptic for open wounds. However, I find that it is advertised widely as a rejuvenator for old age. I want to deal with this matter for a moment. This advertisement reads as follows:
Doctors report "Miracle" royal jelly may change your whole life.
I may say that this is a full page advertisement. It continues:
Here is the thrilling story of royal jelly . . . bringing new hope to countless thousands of men and women over 35 ... by William Duval- 57071-3-251
Supply-Health and Welfare An amazing scientific discovery, just recently made available through the combined efforts of scientists who have, after years of testing in medical laboratories, developed this wonderful substance in combination with eight important and essential vitamins in an easy-to-take capsule form. The powers of royal jelly have been tested over many years. Each year has seen new developments, new proof, as men and women from many countries of the world have begun to feel the amazing benefits of this highly beneficial queen bee's food.
Judging from the amount that is being sold today, there must be a great many queen bees in Canada. The advertisement continues:
(The price of royal jelly was quoted as high as $5.00 per ounce in its initial introduction to the U.S.) Now, thanks to the tireless efforts of research scientists, a way has been found to make this wonder working miracle food of the queen bee available to the public in comparatively inexpensive, easy-to-take, oral capsule form.
Then to quote briefly again-it is a very long advertisement and I am not going to go into all of it-there is a paragraph which reads as follows:
Leading medical authorities in France, England and Germany attest that royal jelly contains vital nutritional factors necessary to the health and well-being of mammals. Royal jelly has been acclaimed as one of the richest natural sources of vigour and vitality.
Discoverer of insulin Dr. Frederick Banting- This is the part to which I wish to direct attention. I wonder whether these statements are true. I am raising the matter because I want the department to go into it and to let us know the truth on this question.
The most complete scientific report on Royal Jelly was prepared under the direction of Dr. Frederick Banting, the discoverer of insulin, at the Banting Institute in Canada. Royal jelly was found to be rich in proteins and vitamins, with a particularly high concentration of pantothenic acid, the vitamin of the important B-Complex group, that has to do with increasing the life span in animals.
Then there is this statement:
"Texas A & M College has been conducting experiments on royal jelly-"
"Professor G. F. Townsend of Ontario agricultural college is resuming research on royal jelly-"
If I had known that, I would have taken the matter up under the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture as well. I just discovered it. This last paragraph to which I wish to direct attention reads as follows:
Royal Jelly may mean "new life" after 35. Reports from Europe tell us of an 80 year old gentleman whose physical condition would make a 50 year old envious.
That is what strikes me.
The man regularly partakes of royal jelly. According to a book published in England, when Russian officials sent questionnaires to all the centenarians (people over 100 years old) in the Soviet union, more than half of them turned out to be beekeepers.

Supply-Health and Welfare
If this is true, not only is this matter of great importance to the Department of National Health and Welfare but it would be of great advantage to the Department of Agriculture and to the beekeepers in general. In any event, I am not going to read further from this advertisement, because the further I read the more I find that my years are dropping away like petals from a rose until I imagine I am returning to my budding youth and possibly going back to rompers again.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because these advertisements are increasing in number. I find only to a limited extent have the advertisements appeared in western papers or periodicals. This advertisement mentions a small quantity for $5 a bottle, a larger quantity for $10 and a little bit larger quantity for $15 and the full double strength size for $20 a bottle. I know people who are buying bottles of this preparation at $20 a bottle in the belief that it is doing their health a great deal of good. I do not know, nor did the people who have written to me and have inquired, whether or not this is a fraud and whether people are being taken advantage of or whether there is some scientific basis for the claims made in these advertisements that recommend it in some cases as a cosmetic, in other cases as a food for the skin, in other cases as an antiseptic for open wounds and, finally, in the majority of cases as a rejuvenator for older people. I think the public should know the truth.
I mention this matter because the administration of the Food and Drugs Act and the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act comes under a certain branch of the minister's department. I know that department does excellent work. It is concerned about the purity of drugs. It is concerned about adulteration, about poisons and things of that sort. I therefore presume that the Department of National Health and Welfare has a full knowledge of this royal jelly and possibly has thoroughly investigated it. I have raised the matter in the house, Mr. Chairman, in order that the people of Canada will have the opportunity to know the truth with respect to the advertised advantages of royal queen bee jelly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of my remarks I want to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare on the manner in which he introduced his estimates. It is certainly not an easy task to follow the steps of a predecessor who was in charge of this department for nearly eleven years and who directed its activity with such a high degree of ability, devotion to duty and consideration for public welfare.

The hon. member for Essex East deserves the gratitude of the Canadian people on more than one count. He devoted his great energies as well as his wide knowledge in the field of public welfare to the establishment and improvement of social measures that affect directly all Canadians from sea to sea. I do not wish to imply that everything the Liberal government did was perfect. On the other hand, no one can deny that it was a Liberal government that laid the foundations for our present system of social security. The least we can ask of the present administration, it seems to me, is that they continue to improve upon it.
I do not wish to join the ranks of the prophets but it seems to me that everyone admits today that as we progress in other fields we must at the same time continue to extend our social legislations as our economic conditions warrant.
If the two historic parties of our country refuse to accept that fact I think, and I feel this very strongly, that our influence will be very greatly diminished in the future. Whether we like it or not and whether we share that point of view, there are those in our midst in Canada, as in other countries, who turn their capacities for demagogy to their own profit. The ideas which these people express eventually find their way into the minds of the public and unless they are taken into consideration, at least up to the limit of common sense, we could pay dearly for our refusal to treat them seriously. It is in this spirit that I do not hesitate to say that our Liberal charter for social security must be constantly reviewed to make sure that our social legislation takes into account the current needs of the Canadian people. As is stated in the latest declaration of Liberal policies, "with a basic charter which provides a solid basis for the security of all Canadians, we are now entering upon a new phase of welfare legislation." The social tragedies which still mar our society are difficult cases which cannot completely be eliminated. Nevertheless, we must never cease our efforts to remove these social problems.
For this reason I am very happy that five proivnces have agreed to participate in the national hospital insurance plan. It is, however, most regrettable that the present government decided against affording full protection to Canadians by including medical, dental and surgical expenses. If the government had included these categories it would have prevented many Canadians from suffering owing to the lack of financial means to obtain adequate treatment. I am astonished that the government did not very seriously consider the recommendations and suggestions along those lines which were made by certain

Conservative members when they were on this side of the house. I would like also to express my disappointment that the province of Quebec has not yet indicated an interest in this matter. I raise these points in all sincerity and without political prejudice, because of the many thousands of Canadians in my province who are in such great need of assistance under this legislation. I am told that the authorities in Quebec are at the present time studying a plan which will be suitable for our needs, but time is passing and the citizens of Quebec are already helping through their taxes to pay for health insurance in other provinces, from which they themselves do not benefit.
I am not at all jealous of those who profit from this assistance, but I am anxious to see the money earned in my province to a certain extent benefit the people of Quebec. I am sure that all my fellow members from Quebec will have had the unfortunate experience of finding that many residents of Quebec are unable to secure hospital treatment. Unless a person is exceptionally well off, or exceptionally poor, he cannot afford the luxury of hospital treatment without mortgaging his salary for months and even years to come. This is a tragic situation which must be dealt with.
The province of Quebec should be in a position today to submit its plan to the federal government and to undertake preliminary discussions with a view to ending the uncertainty existing in many cases. I repeat that I am not making these remarks in a political partisan spirit, but simply to assist my fellow citizens of Quebec to use for their own advantage and their own welfare the money which they earn by their daily toil.
I wish to make a few suggestions to the minister concerning other social measures which I feel would be an immense service to thousands of Canadians. I think it is urgent to increase the flexibility of the definition of the words "disabled" and "invalid" when dealing with disabled persons seeking assistance. This should be done from a humanitarian point of view, having in mind that there are people who are unable to work more than a few weeks or months a year and who as a result are not able to earn even their bare subsistence. It is very difficult for them and for their families to understand that the strict application of the Disabled Persons Act prevents them from taking advantage of assistance which they need so greatly and to which, in my opinion, they are entitled. I certainly could not be accused of being in bad company in this respect for the Prime Minister, when he was on this side of the chamber, attacked this 57071-3-251J
Supply-Health and Welfare problem as recorded in Hansard of July 27, 1956 at page 6537 and page 6538:
This act provides for dominion and provincial contributions; it provides for the payment of an allowance to those who are totally and permanently disabled as prescribed by the regulations. In my experience, this act is being altogether too rigidly administered. The joker in the act is the section that provides that the definition of total and permanent disablement shall be that definition determined by regulations.
The situation today, in whatever cases have come to my attention, indicates that the basis of interpretation excludes many persons who should be qualified and who should receive the allowance.
If the minister makes these necessary changes he will certainly win the gratitude of those whom he would assist by such action and he would also carry out the wish expressed by the Prime Minister himself. It must be admitted that even if a person is capable of moving and able to take nourishment that does not automatically mean that he is able to earn a living.
Our blind persons' legislation should also be amended. First, the qualifying age should be lowered from 18 to 16 years. There is no excuse for not acceding to this request for these persons who are so terribly handicapped. The government stops paying family allowances when a child reaches the age of 16 and between the ages of 16 and 18, for two long years, blind persons find themselves without any assistance. I will go even further -it is not just a question of the period from age 16. The parents of blind persons need assistance from the very moment medical science establishes the blindness of a child. The educational training and care which must be given to a blind child are expensive in most cases, and it is in that difficult period that the parents are in the greatest need of government assistance.
It is true that blindness allowances are paid jointly by the federal and provincial governments, but it does not seem to me that it would be very difficult to agree on changes at a conference on social legislation.
I also suggest that it would be advisable to raise the exemption on earnings of blind persons without, however, entirely eliminating the means test. The government could, for instance, grant to blind persons the same exemption as is granted to single or married persons under the Income Tax Act. I am informed this would increase from 500 to 600 the number of persons qualifying for assistance under this legislation, and that the extra expense to the government would be a little less than $300,000.
I would also like to mention that the Canadian institute for the blind is of the

Supply*-Health and Welfare opinion that we should grant special allowances to blind persons to assist them in meeting the expenses of a guide.
It does not seem to me that these are exorbitant demands, and I believe they deserve the serious and sympathetic consideration of the minister. Once again I cannot be accused of being in bad company in making this request, because the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, when speaking in this chamber on April 18, 1955, as recorded at page 2933 of Hansard for that date, is reported as having said the following words in connection with the qualifying age for blind persons:
I cannot help thinking that the ages between 16 and 20 are ages of uncertainty. They are the time when boys and girls encounter great difficulties, and begin to wonder where they are going and what the future holds for them. Those are the years when their minds are in some state of turmoil. Surely if we can reduce the eligible age from 21 to 18 years we could reduce it to 16 and give those young persons a break, these children whose education is always more difficult and more expensive, these children who many times must travel long distances to get their education, and must be accompanied in their travels.
I offer these suggestions to the minister in the hope that he will give to these requests, which have the support of one of the most distinguished members of the government, careful consideration.
(Translation):
With regard to old age assistance, Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister could consider the possibility of making the benefits available from age 60 to widows and single women. In many cases, widows are not entitled to benefit from or cannot get the needy mothers' allowance, either because they have no children under 16, or because their husbands have left them the family house, and nothing else. The widow is then forced either to sell her house, in order to eat, or keep the house and look for a job. Many of them, however, are unable, for various reasons to take jobs. The only thing the widow can do is to sell her house, board somewhere, and in few years spend what little she has got out of property painfully acquired by her husband, and find herself in abject poverty.
While I am aware that the government has asked that a study be made of the pension scheme in force in the neighbouring republic, I should like to point out to the minister that right here in Canada very many people find it extremely hard to get by between their retirement at 65 and the age when they begin
[Mr. Brassard (Lapointe).3

to receive the old age pension, at 70. In the first place, many companies have no pension plan, or persons retiring at 65 have not been employed long enough to be entitled to adequate pension. Since the general practice requires that all employees retire at 65, it is imperative that old age pension be payable from the age of retirement, at 65. The government is perfectly aware of the large number of pathetic cases throughout the country, and it is high time something were done to assist these people. Here again, I cannot be accused of keeping bad company for I am very happy to see that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) is occupying his seat. I shall therefore now quote what the hon. member from Toronto (Broadview), who is today our distinguished Minister of Transport, was saying in this house in 1956, when dealing precisely with this same subject. As I open the official record of July 25, 1956, I see on page 6507 the following passage. I shall of course be unable to read it with the same feeling and eloquence for which our Minister of Transport is well known. This is what he said:
-another very serious problem is that faced by workers who reach the age of 65 and are retired, and for whom no pension plan has been available to which they could contribute during their working years, and by which they could support themselves and their families when they are retired.
Some firms have pension plans but unfortunately the great majority do not, and when most workers are retired at 65, they have only the savings which they have been able to lay aside during their working years, after meeting the many obligations which families encounter from time to time. Often a lingering illness or serious accident has reduced those savings to a point where there is little left to live on after the breadwinner of the family has retired. I think we all agree it is obvious that some better method must be found for bridging the gap between 65 and 70 years of age, and for bringing our old age pension more into line with the needs of the great majority of the people who receive it.
It is a pity that the genial Minister of Transport has not also been appointed assistant Minister of National Health and Welfare. And this grievance could be applied in several other fields. In the opposition, we used to see the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, (Mr. Green), who promised us a merchant navy; but he was appointed Minister of Public Works. The former official critic on financial matters is Minister without Portfolio today. And this is obviously the case of several other ministers.
I wish to conclude, to the great satisfaction of my hon. friends, by adding a few remarks on the unemployment assistance program set

up by an act of parliament given royal assent on July 11, 1956. With the exception of Quebec, all provinces of Canada have now signed agreements with the federal government for participation in this plan. This unemployment assistance plan offers many advantages but there is one in particular which I would like to point out. I refer to assistance which should be given to people who do not or no longer receive unemployment insurance benefits either because they have not worked long enough to qualify under the act, or because they have used up the benefit period.
Considering the very difficult period we are going through, the least that can be said is that it is deplorable that so many unemployed who no longer qualiy for benefits are being deprived of assistance which is granted to thousands of other unemployed in the other provinces.
An even more difficult period is predicted for the coming winter, and I wonder how those who have not found any work before next winter will be able to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. It is precisely in hard times such as those we are going through that breadwinners really need assistance, and I cannot help repeating that they should not be deprived of an assistance granted to other Canadians and to which citizens of the province of Quebec have contributed by way of taxes. I wonder if the Minister of National Health and Welfare could not take this up with Quebec government authorities and see if it would not be possible to come to an agreement.
Finally, I merely wish to point out the regrettable fact that the government wilfully neglected to raise the amount of family allowances. When we consider that it has raised all other measures of social security, we wonder at the reasons for this regrettable omission.
In conclusion, may I repeat that all that social legislation was instituted under a Liberal government. I know that this program is not perfect but we must nevertheless recognize that the former administration did blaze the trail in the social field and open new vistas in this regard. Between May 14, 1948 when the Rt. Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King first introduced to the country his public health program, and 1957, the federal government paid over to the provinces close to $225,000,000 in national health assistance. Quebec received somewhat better than 68 millions of this amount. True, there has never
Supply-Health and Welfare been a great deal of noisy publicity in our province in this respect. I felt however that I should bring that fact to the attention of my hon. colleagues. I might add, quite objectively, that Quebec has made good use of those millions, and that we have made great strides in this field. There has been an enormous amount of work done in the field of public health in this country, though a great deal yet remains to be done.
In this regard the government must remain forever watchful since the issue is that of human resources, the most important of all resources in this country. Mr. Mackenzie King, who pioneered this system in Canada, understood the issue fully. He stated, as recorded in Hansard on May 14, 1948, as he introduced this new plan to the house:
But of all the nation's resources, Its human resources are unquestionably the most precious. The preservation in health and strength of its population is surely the best of all guarantees of the nation's power, of its progress and of its prosperity. Our greatest national asset is the health and well-being of our people.
The Liberal government has shown the way. This is a challenge to the Conservative government, at least for so long as it can maintain itself in power-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a very important problem for my constituency. Recently we have been told that the hospital of immigration, property of the federal government situated in my riding, is going to be closed.
I have lately received a resolution from the Quebec regional council of the Canadian federation of civil employees and also a telegram from the Quebec board of trade concerning this event. I take the liberty of reading a few of the numerous items of this resolution that will permit me to shorten my remarks:
Whereas Immigration hospital, 300 Boulevard Hamel, Quebec West, P.Q., is the only federal institution within the limits of Quebec West constituency,
Whereas immigration hospital is still today as well as during the last years in a position to

Supply-Health and Welfare
accept for general or specialized treatments some two hundred and twenty-five patients,
Whereas immigration hospital can supply the most up to date and medically advanced treatments,
Whereas the closing of immigration hospital cannot but bring disastrous effects, morally, economically, as well as socially, directly and immediately on the local and regional area and indirectly at the national level,
Whereas the closing of immigration hospital would deprive some one hundred and fifty actual employees of their jobs,
Whereas the salary paid to these one hundred and fifty employees represents the interesting sum of some four hundred and fifty thousand dollars a year,
Whereas the closing of immigration hospital would deprive our local merchants not only of the purchasing power represented by these employees but also the local purchases made by the hospital administration for the needs of the hospital itself,
Whereas these local purchases would mean to our local merchants a loss of business equal to some one hundred and fifty thousand dollars a year,
Whereas the closing of immigration hospital would mean a total loss of some seven hundred thousand dollars a year to the local and regional business trade,
Whereas the closing of immigration hospital in Quebec West is not and cannot in any way be submitted and/or considered neither actually nor in any event as a logical and recommendable means to check the all-over Canada growing unemployment.
Be it resolved that:
To provide the best possible service to the welfare of Indians and Eskimos,
To maintain to the highest level of efficiency experienced services already existing and devoted to these patients of a different and special type, and this at nominal cost,
To maintain to some one hundred and fifty employees the security of a guaranteed job,
To maintain for the local industry and trade the income meant by some seven hundred thousand dollars a year,
Earnest entreaties be submitted to the minister so that:
Immigration hospital in Quebec West, P.Q., not only avoid closing but be guaranteed permanently its existence as the hospitalization and treatment center for eastern Canada Indians and Eskimos.
I inquired, Mr. Chairman, about the reasons to justify the closing of this hospital. The main reason given is the lack of patients among immigrants and Indians. I was advised that the number of patients would not be sufficient to justify the maintenance of this hospital. I want to agree with the reasons given but here I would like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to delay his decision and allow me to offer a few considerations and suggestions with a view to helping the settlement of this problem to the satisfaction of every one and keeping our hospital open.
The Quebec hospital of immigration is situated in my constituency the population of which comprises 85 per cent labourers and where the unemployment problem is an important one. Consequently this period of unemployment would not be a favourable

time at which to execute such a decision. It would represent a loss in salaries and in all kinds of other benefits to the estimated total value of $700,000 a year. Therefore I urge the minister to take that important economical point of view into consideration.
Let me then offer the minister a few suggestions with the desire of helping him give to my constituency a favourable answer or at least to delay reaching a final decision. I suggest that the hospital of immigration could be used for the centralized treatment of all sick immigrants entering Canada through eastern harbours and of all the Indians of the numerous reserves in our eastern provinces. In doing so the minister could not consider closing the hospital but rather would have to consider enlarging it. I hope this suggestion will be taken into serious consideration but if it is impossible of realization allow me to offer the minister a further suggestion.
In Quebec city, according to a recent investigation, we require at least 1,200 additional hospital beds to satisfy our needs. The problem is particularly serious for our general practitioners and family doctors who can scarcely find beds for their patients in the general hospitals where the number of beds is insufficient for the medical staff of specialized doctors. Consequently, our family doctors often cannot be admitted to attend their patients in our hospitals and may be rather considered as ambulance drivers.
Mr. Chairman, our general practitioners, our family doctors, must still be considered the pillars of the medical profession, those who are always ready to render service day and night, seven days a week, and we should assist and encourage them to continue in the highly important medico-social role they play among our people. In the light of the present trend there is a great danger of seeing them disappear to follow their colleagues into specialized fields. The cost of medical treatment is prohibitive today because of over-specialization. Consequently I suggest to the minister that he keep open the Quebec hospital of immigration and put its unoccupied beds at the disposal of labouring peoples to facilitate their treatment by family doctors in this area.
I take pleasure in mentioning the sympathetic feelings of the premier of the province of Quebec toward family doctors and I dare to say that an agreement should be possible with our provincial government in that direction.
I am very happy to offer the Minister of National Health and Welfare my contribution as a general practitioner and a member of the government party to bring about such an

Private Bills
agreement. In this connection we see on the one hand a lack of patients when compared with the great number of beds available and, on the other hand, there is a lack of hospital beds in comparison with the number of our patients. One should meet the other on the same ground. Is this not a peculiar position to be in when we are trying to take the first step to arrive at an agreement between the federal and Quebec provincial governments in regard to the problem of hospital insurance? We know that the realization of that goal depends upon hospital beds and it will be difficult to realize it when there is a lack of hospital beds. Therefore, I ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to delay his decision to close this hospital and, in the meantime, let us hear a few words of hope and encouragement for the benefit of my constituents, the patients and the family doctors.
I would like to close my remarks by offering another suggestion to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The difficulty of reaching an agreement with the province of Quebec in so far as a hospitalization plan is concerned is brought about by a lack of hospital beds, as I said a minute ago. The number of hospital beds would be probably sufficient if the beds were occupied by those who need to be hospitalized. Consequently, a patient should not be admitted to a hospital unless the diagnosis is made by a medical practitioner, with the help of the diagnostic service. If we admit all cases then tiresome people will be admitted to the hospitals. According to investigations that have been made almost one-third of our hospital beds are occupied by people who have subscribed to Blue Cross hospital insurance plans or similar plans. The beds are occupied by people who should be treated at home by their family doctors. I suggest that at the next session of parliament we should study the possibility of amending the hospital insurance law to limit hospitalization to people who need to be hospitalized. If there is no control on the admittance of people to hospitals the cost of the hospitalization insurance plan will be fantastic. We will have to build an enormous number of hospitals to accommodate those who would like to be hospitalized for everything and nothing.
To those who are concerned about the position of Quebec in the hospital scheme may I say that I have talked to the premier of our province about the problem of hospitalization insurance under the federal plan. I believe the premier of our province is considering the possibility of Quebec entering into the federal plan. Everybody who knows our province knows that our premier is wise and
prudent. As he said, no man can open a grocery store if he has nothing to put on his shelves. Therefore, we will be ready to enter the federal hospitalization insurance plan when we have beds to offer to the patients. At the present time the province of Quebec is following the policy of building hospitals, regional hospitals, in almost all of our constituencies so that very soon the premier will be in a position to enter the federal scheme. I am sure that the plan will cover not only general diseases but mental and tuberculosis diseases as well, also the infirm and the incurable. I hope that when that day comes our friends who are concerned about the intentions of our premier will be satisfied.

In rising to discuss this particular bill, Mr. Chairman, I do not need to emphasize the fact that the problem of divorce in parliament has been a problem for quite a length of time. In this case, I believe, the petitioner was domiciled in Montreal at the time of the marriage, and the respondent was an immigrant from Germany who had just recently come to Canada. In scanning the evidence quickly, some doubt was raised in my mind as to whether or not evidence had been given to establish the domicile of the respondent so, in a sense, the question of our jurisdiction in this particular matter is raised. I say that because apparently the respondent has not taken out Canadian citizenship papers, and so far as I can see no evidence has been adduced before the Senate committee as to his intention of staying in Canada or whether he is planning to return to Germany.
In my opinion, there has not been any evidence to establish whether or not he is actually domiciled in Canada or in Germany. With this particular doubt being raised in my mind, we are faced with the additional difficulty of whether or not parliament should be considering divorce at all in view of its already onerous schedule when we are already sitting every evening and on Saturday all day-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When I was mentioning the hours of sitting, I was doing so in order to highlight the fact that the house has to devote its very valuable time to the discussion of matters of divorce. I feel that the divorce committee, although it is comprised of lawyers who have certain qualifications with regard to this matter, was not in a position to give full consideration to these facts that are before us. I feel that we should again consider this important question of whether or not these bills should be referred at all to parliament because-
Private Bills-Divorce

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
In discussing Bill No. SD-267, may I say that unfortunately in my mind it brings out the difficulties that I am bringing forward. In Bill No. SD-267 we have the usual situation of the investigators this time going into an apartment building and finding the respondent and the woman named in certain, shall we say, unfortunate circumstances. To my own mind, without referring to this particular bill, there is a certain difficulty as to whether the situation is one that we can believe, in a sense; because to my mind it rather stretches the credulity of the average person living in the world when he considers the number of such situations.
We are faced with a situation in Canada where the divorce laws provide the basis, as in this particular case, of adultery, except in some of the other provinces such as British Columbia and the maritimes where the basis can be rape, sodomy or bestiality. Yet if we were to be honest and go behind the actual idea or the reason for the particular divorce we may find a situation where there is actual cruelty, desertion or some other equally logical sociological reason for a divorce. Yet because of the archaic ideas inflicted by the other provinces on parliament we are placed in the situation that two people desiring to get separated must say: What have we to do in order to get a divorce? The answer of the lawyer is adultery. The second question is: How are we able to get that evidence? The result then is that parliament, although it has complete flexibility as to what it could do in the matter of divorce,-because parliament can do anything-has adopted the basis of adultery. It could just as logically take as the basis perhaps the colour of the petitioner's eyes. In other words, if the petitioner's eyes were blue we could, I suggest, with the evidence placed before us and the opportunity we have to investigate it, grant a divorce just as logically. If parliament is going to adopt adultery as a basis, I would suggest that from the economic point of view I fail to see the necessity for two people who are anxious to get separated, and who are going to get separated regardless of any obstacles, having to do anything to simulate adultery if the basis suggested by parliament is adultery. In all seriousness I suggest that we should have a mimeographed form leaving blank a place for the name of the husband or wife, the age of the couple, when they were married, the marriage certificate and perhaps we

could leave blank the name of the apartment, hotel or motel where the adultery was committed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I regret, Mr. Chairman, that I was perusing this bill rather quickly and am unable to put my finger on the exact spot. But I wonder whether the chairman could answer, in connection with the matter of the actual problem of adultery, as to what there is in the evidence indicating that there actually was adultery or what corroboration there was on the part of the two detectives to establish this adultery?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this was not a one-night stand by the respondent with some woman, as perhaps had been suggested in the remarks of the hon. member earlier. The evidence is that the couple were separated, that the husband had gone off to live with another woman and that the two investigators in this particular case had gone to the apartment where they were living in Montreal and verified these facts at a late hour in the evening. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The only evidence of any adultery was the fact that the two people were in the same building at the same time. They were both clothed at the time, were they not?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In your opinion, Mr. Chairman, does the fact that the woman was wearing blue and white pyjamas and that the man was wearing a dark dressing gown constitute adultery?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been told about the birds and the bees as have the hon. member and all other hon. members of the house. The principles of law that are followed by the Senate committee and by the committee of the Commons are exactly those principles of law that are used in any court in the provinces where they have divorce jurisdiction or divorce practices. That principle is that when couples are found in a position which indicates that it is more probable that they are committing adultery than that they are not committing adultery, and you infer from the evidence that adultery

has been committed. Then you can make a finding of adultery that will justify the dissolution of the marriage.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would you not find in this particular situation, as in the majority of divorce cases you are reviewing, that apart from the fact that you are in the divorce committee the factors involved would, shall we say, stretch the credulity of a reasonable man as to the question of adultery? Does the hon. member believe that in the majority of these situations-as in this particular case-adultery was actually committed, or is the evidence of such nature that the committee feels that it is close enough so that they can give the couple a divorce, which of course is the objective? I would suggest that perhaps the question of whether or not they had blue eyes or brown hair would be equally as good from an evidentiary point of view.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I would not think that the question of whether they had blue eyes or brown hair would have any particular bearing on the matter, but before the hon. member got to the latter part of his question he did make what I thought was a good point. That is, if you find a couple together in an apartment, motel or hotel on any occasion, you automatically assume that because one happens to be a man and the other happens to be a woman they are therefore going to commit adultery within the next few hours or have just done so before they were discovered. Then, I suppose, there is a fictional inference which has crept into the law, that if people are found living together over a period of time it may be assumed that they have committed adultery on any one occasion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If the matter of the committing of adultery is fictional, then does the committee have discretion? speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. SD-289, for the relief of Robena Sarah Florence Worrell Day-Mr. McCleave-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This is the petition of Robena Sarah Florence Worrell Day for a bill of divorce from Warren Day. I did wish to speak on the principles involved, but I will confine my remarks to the evidence which came before the committee.
As has been outlined by other hon. members, the rule of evidence in divorce cases is the civic rule of probability, and I find it hard from reading the evidence in this case to be fully convinced purely on the grounds of probability that there was, in fact, adultery free of the three general requisites in matters of this kind. These requisites are firstly, that the adultery should be free of collusion; secondly, that it should be free of condonement; and, thirdly, that it should be free of connivance. I think we can rule out connivance, because I do not see any evidence or suggestion that these two persons ever got together and agreed to adultery on the part of either one. In view of the fact that the husband did not appear to defend this suit, I am led to believe that there was no connivance, because he would have appeared to try to make the case, shall we say, more binding if connivance had existed.
I think, however, that perhaps there was condonement. These two persons lived together, according to the evidence, for some 14 or 15 years, and although the wife claims the marriage was a happy one, I think the evidence shows clearly that it was not happy after the first four years. It is my opinion that moral lapses do not suddenly occur at the age of 40. If this man was continually drinking, was a night hawk and was running around with other women, I think that would have been evident years before this time. The wife is a nurse and she said that throughout her married life she had worked. It appears to me she was an independent woman and that she in fact never did make a home for this man. I would not say she drove him to drink, but he did drink from

Private Bills-Divorce
the early days of his marriage, and there is no evidence that she did anything to try to cure him of these habits. When he stayed out late at nights over a period of years, she apparently made no effort to resolve the differences between them.
The husband was a capable tradesman earning a good income, and the wife apparently never questioned him about his income except in so far as she said he drank too much. She kept on working and I would say she probably supported the home. They therefore lived apart in spirit for many years before they decided to dissolve the marriage.
For this reason I think there was probably condonement for a number of years. There is no evidence before the committee as to the moral record of the woman, which is relevant in a case of divorce, because I think it is against the wishes of the people of Canada to grant divorce where, in fact, people are living immoral lives and condoning it.
I say there is no evidence of connivance, or open connivance, but it does seem strange to me that after these years of married life action should suddenly be taken. They have a daughter 17 years of age who, incidentally, is herself married at that early age, which suggests lack of parental care. After 18 or 19 years of married life they have agreed to disagree.
They were married in New Brunswick and I would not contest the domicile in Quebec, for they have certainly lived in Quebec over a period of years, but here again the evidence is merely negative. I do not challenge the jurisdiction of the courts to try this case, because I understand that a federal statute being involved, it has been the practice to allow the Senate regardless of domicile to hear divorce cases. This is a question, of course, which would have to be decided on constitutional grounds, and perhaps some day we may have a case-and I think we should have-to clear up this problem, because, as all hon. members will realize, a divorce obtained in this manner leads to many domestic problems.
If these two people, having their divorce, were to argue about the future care of the children and the question of their support, this could not be decided in the federal courts. It has to go to the provinces but which province they should go to is a moot question. The fact that they had their divorce as residents of Quebec does not mean to say the Quebec court can necessarily solve those difficulties.
As to collusion-the intentional misleading of the court-I do not think there is evidence here to show that either of these parties intended to mislead the court by the evidence produced, but my objection to this
tMr. Bigg.]
particular case is that the evidence is very scanty, and we appear to be granting a divorce on the very minimum of evidence. I should like to have had some evidence on the living habits, the drinking habits and the moral habits of both these parties. It is difficult to argue about the right of granting these divorces unless we discuss principles, but I should like to suggest that we should be very careful about granting divorces on such slim grounds. The evidence in this case covers only some five pages, and here we are taking it upon ourselves to dissolve the most serious contract a man or a woman can enter into-that of marriage. And though it may seem a waste of the time of the committee or of the Senate or of this house, this is a very serious matter indeed to dissolve a marriage which was entered into, I trust, with all the hope and faith required to make a marriage good. I, for one, were I sitting on a bench, if this matter had been brought before me in a provincial court would, I am sure, have wished to have had more evidence on the grounds I have mentioned before I put my name to the dissolving of this contract.
Again, about condonement I should like to say that I think a woman can condone the adultery of her husband as well by keeping quiet as by giving consent. If she knows that her husband is running around with other women I think it is her duty as a wife and mother to complain on the first occasion she finds this going on. There is no need to wait until 2.30 in the morning before making some inquiries about her husband's habits. I do not think a woman could live with a man for 14 years and not know whether he was committing adultery or not. I do not know that refusing to make a man's home as pleasant as possible can be called condonement, but it is certainly driving a man to seek happiness elsewhere.
As to the evidence whether or not the respondent and the lady concerned actually committed adultery, again I am not convinced. When the private detectives came to the suite the lights were out at 11.30. They knocked on the door and they declared themselves. The husband came to the door. It was true he was barefooted, but that is not any evidence and I should like to suggest-and I think hon. members will agree with me-that the fact that he came to the door after the men rapped and said they were private detectives, and that he was caught in this compromising position, is not without significance because unless he wanted a divorce he would, I think, have got properly dressed. He had no need to come to the door and answer the call of a private detective unless he knew that by opening

that door he would give his wife, for whom he probably had little regard for by then, the usual evidence necessary. So far as he was concerned he was providing the courts with the evidence with the least possible delay or trouble. I cannot believe anything else. I also doubt very much whether the lady in question was in fact there to commit adultery. There is no evidence at all that her dress was removed. She held the bed clothes up to her chin, I suggest, quite possibly to hide the fact that she was still properly dressed just as much as to indicate that she was improperly dressed. She knew that the detectives were coming in, and any young woman who would allow herself to be put into this compromising position need have no great modesty.
A man with the experience I have had in law enforcement knows that when you go into a brothel the young ladies are not at all modest. They are, in fact, generally proud of their profession. I cannot believe, from the limited evidence I have seen in this case, that there was in fact adultery, although I will say that there was certainly every opportunity for adultery. If there was anything to be gained by this man getting rid of a wife whom he had long since ceased to regard, I myself would believe that adultery had probably been committed. But the doubt arises from the fact that both the husband and the wife were anxious to be clear of each other, and this suggests to me that they either condoned adultery or that they were, in fact, behind the scenes in collusion.
The Senate committee has had a great deal of experience in these matters and they are up against a serious problem. I would not ask to have this divorce bill held up because I realize that the committee was not in this case breaking up a marriage in a true sense; we are merely allowing two people to separate legally where no real marriage has ever existed. Therefore, I would not ask to have this bill held up. I would ask, however, that we should take the greatest of care in seeing that we have the fullest evidence possible on every occasion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Not yet. I am sorry to see facts brought out in this way, because this is the type of discussion which could more profitably go on in committee behind closed doors so that we do not hurt people, particularly the children involved. But several points have been raised by the hon. member and they are going to be dealt with.
First, the question of domicile. Domicile in the province of Quebec was clearly established for 16 years.
Private Bills-Divorce
Secondly, the support of the children: the husband is paying $40 a month in respect of the child.
Thirdly, the question of the garb of the people found in the suite by the detectives. There was evidence of their underclothing being found under the bed.
I may add that the question of the home conditions and the husband's habits are clearly set forth in the evidence at the bottom of page 10 and the top of page 11.
Then, as to the matter of collusion or condonation, the fact is that the wife has signed and sworn to a petition presented to parliament which makes serious allegations, and the husband has not seen fit to come before the committee of the other place, or before the committee of this house to deny those allegations, and that is something which must properly be taken into account.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to disagree with anything said by the hon. member for Athabasca because of his experience in the fields of investigation and police work. But I believe he is requiring a standard of proof that is quite unwarranted. The circumstances in this particular case were certainly incriminating although not conclusive. We never find positive evidence in a divorce case. People do not engage in these questionable activities in public and they take due precautions to see that they do have some privacy. All we can hope for is some evidence from which we can draw a reasonable conclusion that adultery did in fact take place. I suggest there is more than sufficient evidence in this case to warrant that conclusion. I turn to the report of the committee of the other place. At page 14 I should like to read from the interrogation by Mr. Jacobs of the investigator, Mr. Brault:
Q. I show you a photograph which has been filed as exhibit 2, can you identify the person?
A. Mr. Warren Day.
Q. Were you with Mr. Etheridge, on January 9, 1958, when you saw this person you have identified?
Incidentally, Mr. Etheridge was the accompanying investigator. I continue:
A. Yes, I was on surveillance on January 9, 1958 at five o'clock with Mr. Etheridge in the vicinity of 1863 Dorchester west. At 6.15 Warren Day arrived in his car with a woman and parked his car at St. Mark street, and the woman was wearing a muskrat brown coat with kerchief, and he was wearing a brown coat and brown hat.
Warren Day is the respondent in the case. I continue:
They went to 1863 Dorchester in apartment 11. At 7.45 Mr. Etheridge and I left the place to go on some other work, and we came back at 11.30. speechtext:
I had just had time, Mr. Chairman, to extend congratulations to the minister when the committee rose at five o'clock for the consideration of public and private bills. I had, I believe, observed that for the first time the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare had passed the $1 billion mark. I believe the minister gave the exact figure as $1,180,089,181 to which we must add approximately $70 million more for payments it is expected will be made under the health insurance and diagnostic services plan to those provinces who have put the plan into effect on July 1. Altogether, this makes a total expenditure of approximately $1.25 billion, actually, $1,250,089,181. The minister pointed out that 92 per cent of these expenditures are statutory, but nevertheless they are expenditures and the money must be found to cover them.
The bulk of these expenditures will be made on various forms of welfare services, health grants and so on. I should like to point out to the committee that the Department of National Health and Welfare is not the only department which spends money for these kinds of services. In our estimates we find that the Department of Veterans Affairs is also spending $291,882,345 for services which are very similar to those provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare. These services provided by the Department of Veterans Affairs cover health grants, health services, diagnostic services, welfare payments and pensions, which are very similar to those covered by the Department of National Health and Welfare. If we add the expenditures of these two departments together, we get approximately $1.5 billion which this federal government is spending on these kinds of services, services which we usually include within the term social security.
If we look at our estimates for national defence, we find that we are spending approximately $1.68 billion for national defence. Our expenditures for social security, therefore,
Supply-Health and Welfare are approximately equal to our expenditures for national security. There has been a great deal of concern expressed in various parts of Canada, and in the committee on estimates, as to the capacity of the Canadian economy to support this burden. I think if it is logical to express concern over the burden of national defence, it is equally logical to express concern over the burden of social security, which is approximately equal. Next year, when the full cost of health insurance and diagnostic services is felt, there will be very little difference between what we spend on social security and what we spend on national defence.
One of the large items under the Department of National Health and Welfare is the expenditure on old age assistance. Yesterday the minister, in replying to a question which I had on the order paper, supplied me with information which showed that from July, 1957, to July, 1958 inclusive the payments made under the old age assistance plan exceeded the revenue by $154,098,080. Now, if the royal jelly which our good friend from Kootenay West spoke about this afternoon becomes available to our old age pensioners and they get rejuvenated from 70 years down to 50 years, we are going to be faced with a financing problem of great magnitude to keep this fund solvent. The revenues for this old age security plan come from taxes which have been allocated for that special purpose, two per cent of the corporation tax, two per cent of the sales tax and two per cent of the income tax up to a maximum of $60. However, these revenues have not been sufficient to keep this fund solvent in times of recession. When the corporation taxes and sales taxes decline, the gap between revenue and payments is bound to widen. Some other method, therefore, must be found to keep this fund solvent.
In order to keep this fund solvent now the government has made loans. This cannot be continued indefinitely and the time is not far distant when some other method will have to be found to finance these old age payments. I should like to ask the minister what consideration is being given to providing the necessary funds in order to keep this fund solvent. I should like to suggest to him that this would be a first-rate time to consider the development of a national pension plan, a plan which would be developed through the co-operation of government labour and industry as well as other interested agencies, a plan which would be put on a sound financial basis and which would provide pensions based on contributions. These pensions could be transferred from one occupation to another or from one part of the country to another. I know there

Supply-Health and Welfare is a Professor Clark who is making a study of the old age pension plans which obtain in the United States, but that is not the same thing as I understand it. I think we must revise our thinking on the ways and means of keeping this fund solvent. The present is a very good time in which to set up the necessary machinery to get all the information we require and to see what can be done to bring in a national pension plan.
I should also like to say a few words about the disability pensions. I am going to be brief because they were covered fairly well this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Lapointe. However, there is a problem in connection with the administration of these pensions. There are three factors which must be taken into account. The first factor revolves around the interpretation of the term "totally and permanently disabled". That term is subject to a wide variety of opinions and interpretations which vary from board to board and from province to province. Another factor is the financial position of the province which is administering these pensions. As I understand it, the federal government pays only half and the other half must come out of the provincial treasury. If the province is having a difficult time financially and must retrench, then of course they are going to be restricted in the amount of money actually which can be allocated to these disability pensions; and that consideration in turn will restrict the number of people who can receive them.
I think the administration of these disability pensions should be taken out of the hands of the provincial government and should be administered completely by the federal government. I admit that whatever we do it cannot be perfect. We shall always have borderline cases from which we can never escape. Nevertheless, I think more can be done than has been done up until now to set up criteria which will enable uniform administration of these pensions. Otherwise we are going to be faced with a situation where a person who lives in one province might qualify for a disability pension whereas a person with exactly the same disability and living in another province cannot do so. I think that is something that all hon. members in this house would wish to avoid.
Before I sit down, Mr. Chairman, I should like to put to the minister two questions which I hope he will answer, in addition to those which I have already posed. This morning the minister mentioned a sum of money- I did not quite catch it as he read it out- or the expenditure which has been provided

for in connection with unemployment assistance payments; I refer to those to ablebodied persons owing to the removal of the floor. When he replies, I should like the minister to tell us just how much money has been spent on that item up until now and how the money has been distributed among the ten provinces of Canada.
The minister also mentioned his attendance at the world health organization. We were very happy to learn that Canada is taking such a great interest and playing such an important part in the great work of this organization. The minister told us that the budget which had been prepared for the work of the world health organization was, I believe, $15 million. When he replies I should be glad if he would tell us just how much Canada has contributed to that $15 million budget.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There are only a few comments I should like to make. One of them is on a matter which has been discussed by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I refer to the matter of disability pensions. In the province of Ontario we have a good deal of difficulty in the administration of these pensions and the requirements that must be met before pension can be established. In Ontario it became an act from which very few people ever received any benefit. It is generally understood that in order to receive the disability pension in the province of Ontario you must be permanently and totally disabled. If you have one foot you can put on the floor, you are not classed as being permanently and totally disabled.
The other day a lady who is connected with welfare work in my riding brought to my attention the names of three young girls who are now graduated from school. One is an epileptic, another is a "polio" victim and the third is similarly disabled. These girls are not able to work. In my opinion, they always will be disabled and quite badly so. They are able to look after themselves; therefore they do not come under this disability pension. In a country as rich as Canada I think consideration can be given to persons of this type. They are not completely helpless. In this case two of the girls are quite capable of doing certain types of work, but those types of work are normally not available in the area in which they live. If they go some place else there is going to be the matter of looking after them for at least some time so far as money for living and becoming established is concerned. I think much more can be done in this field of helping the disabled people across Canada, particularly the young people who have no other means of support and who can look forward to 30 years, 40 years

or 50 years of dependence on their parents or on welfare organizations for a livelihood. I think Canada is quite capable of financing a much better deal for disabled persons.
Another problem is in connection with those people 40 years or 50 years old-yes, and some much younger-who are afflicted with a heart ailment which leaves them, as far as investigators are concerned, in a very healthy condition and yet medical advice is to the effect that they are permanently and totally disabled. In many cases they are able to walk down town on good days and to get around and they look quite healthy but from a medical point of view they are completely disabled. In most cases these people do not meet the requirements laid down by the province of Ontario in the administration of this act. I think the requirements by the federal government, in the joint negotiations they hold in setting up the requirements for this act, could be made much more lenient so that more of the people who are deserving cases could see some future for themselves without depending strictly on welfare agencies.
Another problem that has been mentioned by many others-and I do not want to belabour the point-is the fact that we have not yet decided that we are going to keep our social security on a standard in keeping with today's cost of living. The family allowance, the old age pension, the disabled persons pension and the other social security measures that we enjoy in Canada I do not believe were granted before an election or with that event in view. They were developed over many years and have been granted as a fair and reasonable amount in each case. When the family allowance was introduced it was worth twice as much as it is today, and we have not seen fit to tie in our social security measures with the cost of living so that we may maintain the standard of living originally intended, which would be the only way in which the Canadian citizens could receive the benefits which the legislation was originally expected to provide.
The family allowance is limited to children under the age of 16 years, but all parents are well aware of the fact that rather than being able to do without this assistance when their children reach this age, more money is necessary at that time in order to provide for higher education. I think this government would be well advised to introduce legislation to extend family allowances for the benefit of those parents who wish to send their children to high school, even up to the age of 21 years, if they desire to continue their education. Such a measure would do much to alleviate the problems with which many families are faced when
Supply-Health and Welfare their children reach the age 16 or 17. They have to provide them with suitable clothing and all the other things which are necessary to ensure a background and environment in keeping with a desired standard of living.
I would also recommend that more research work be done by the department into such matters as industrial diseases. I mentioned this matter last year and I would emphasize the importance of this question, particularly in so far as mines are concerned. I have in mind those mines containing silica dust and now the mines in the new field of uranium. International organizations are finding that close proximity to uranium ore is causing genetic problems which we did not even realize existed a few years ago. I believe the government has an obligation to carry out research work and to implement recommendations along the lines suggested as a result of investigations. Precautions should be taken, particularly in the case of those companies which have so far not been too co-operative with respect to the welfare of their workers.
In the field of cancer, I think the department should spend a great deal more money on research. We read in the newspapers and in the medical journals that many investigators in this field believe they are now on the verge of solving some of the problems connected with this disease. The scientists are undertaking experiments which are disclosing developments believed to have significant effects upon cancer. In Canada scientists have developed certain protections, particularly at the research institute in Toronto. If more money and assistance could be made available to research scientists in this field by the federal government it is quite possible that this problem might be solved as were the problems of tuberculosis and other diseases. It is to be hoped, therefore, that the government will put its shoulder to the wheel in this respect.
One other matter I would like to raise at this time is a matter which I do not believe should come under the jurisdiction of this department, and that is the matter of civil defence. Unless there are some significant findings as a result of the investigations which I understand are now taking place, I would strongly recommend that the minister transfer the administration with respect to civil defence to the Department of National Defence. Adequate instruction has not been given to the Canadian people with respect to such matters as basic first aid training which will be vital in case of disaster. In the case of first aid training, of course, jurisdiction should remain with the Department of National Health and Welfare, and it will do so, but with respect to the other aspects of

Supply-Health and Welfare civil defence I feel that the administration should be returned to the Department of National Defence, particularly having regard to implications in the event of an atomic attack. The majority of the Canadian people are completely unaware of even the basic requirements for their protection in the case of atomic warfare. The government has seen fit in recent weeks to spend huge sums of money to popularize the idea of the conversion of one type of bond for another, but I believe that this money could be spent in a way more beneficial to our people if we were to give them the basic training for protection against radiation.
If we consider it important to consider such things as moving our national capital from one place to another, then surely we should consider the threat of this type of warfare. As long as this threat is with us we have an obligation to at least give the Canadian people the rudiments of first aid training so that they may have some chance of protecting themselves in an emergency.

speechtext:
I wish to say a few words in this debate, both in a desire to obtain some information and to point out a few difficulties which I believe will arise in connection with our national hospital insurance plan. I very much regret that the province of Prince Edward Island seems to have lost all interest in health insurance, and I would like to inquire of the minister whether he has recently received any communication from the government of my province.
I would also like to draw the attention of the house to a condition which will affect many of our citizens after January 1, 1959, and that is with regard to those people who are carrying private hospitalization schemes as a supplement to provincial hospital plans. Perhaps we could take Ontario as an example. The Ontario plan provides public ward hospitalization, nursing care, operating room, X-ray, physiotherapy, laboratory and also covers most drugs, but many people find the idea of admission to a public ward rather disturbing, and they therefore attempt to cover the difference in cost by carrying an insurance policy.
As I understand it, if a semi-private patient or a private patient, when this plan comes into effect, goes into hospital, and if by reason of a shortage of beds he has to go into a public ward, he will receive no compensation whatever from his insurance company. Before the Ontario plan was in operation the difference between the public ward cost and private or semi-private ward cost was paid to the patient by the insurance company. For example, let us say a patient
[Mr. Peters.l
had an insurance policy providing $15 a day. If the patient was in a ward which cost $10 a day he would receive the difference between the $10 and the $15 from the insurance company. That is only fair, and it is hard to understand how anyone who has taken out these insurance policies finds that he will receive nothing from the insurance company despite the fact that he has paid the insurance premium could feel that his foresight had been justified.
Another point with regard to health insurance is that the rates vary from hospital to hospital within a province. A number of insurance companies have had plans paying a stated sum per day regardless of the hospital rate. This, I understand, must be discontinued after January 1, as the amount will be cut to the average between ward and semi-private and private rooms, that is, the provincial average, and it appears that some of the insurance companies are going out of this type of business. I do not think the government when it introduced national health insurance had the idea of forcing these insurance companies out of the business.
Several members have already pointed out that the hospital insurance scheme will result in an increased demand for hospital beds. In addition to that, we in Canada have approximately six million people under the age of 20, and a rapidly increasing population. The increased grants for hospital and construction, especially those for chronic care, are a step in the right direction, and I suggest to the minister that he keep a sharp eye on hospital construction costs with the idea that if they increased very much more a further increase will be required.
One matter which is a source of irritation to various hospital boards is the delay when an application is made for a construction grant. One small hospital in my constituency has had an application before the provincial government for almost two years and no action has been taken on it. After they have obtained approval from the provincial government they must obtain federal approval and I should like to suggest to the minister that a joint committee of the provincial and federal governments be set up to try to eliminate these delays.
The cost of hospital insurance for a full year will not be known for some time. I have fears that the final cost will be a bit of a financial shock to the taxpayers, and in order to keep the cost in line with reality it may be advisable to have a patient pay a small sum on admission, say $25 or the first three days toward the cost of hospitalization. This would prevent unnecessary admissions to

hospital and would reduce the demand for hospital beds. In addition it would also be of great assistance to the practising physician as he would not be subject to undue pressure from patients who desire hospital treatment in cases where they could probably be treated equally well at home.
