Mr. Chairman, near though we are to the end of the session, with each member preparing to return to his constituency, I cannot miss this opportunity of expressing a few heartfelt views on civil defence and family allowances, while we are on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Regarding civil defence, Mr. Chairman, I know you will understand my placing special emphasis on the requirements of the Montrealers. As councillor for the city of Montreal-Canada's metropolis-I was in a firsthand position to witness what was done in this field by those then responsible, particularly from 1950 to 1954, when Brigadier Guy Gauvreau was co-ordinator.
As we all know, the world is going through frantic and distracting times as a result of scientific developments which give us Russian sputnik one day, an American rocket another day and today, they are talking of conquering the moon. What lies in store for us tomorrow? Heaven only knows. That is why today government departments must, at all costs, join and work with a common aim, so as to bring home to each and every Canadian the necessity of his making sacrifices in order to organize civil defence, forestall disaster, and save as many human lives as possible

for the enemy is looking for modern methods to annihilate us.
Montreal, with a population of over a million and a half, is entitled to federal aid to supplement its contribution. As I was saying a few minutes ago, some progress has already been made in this direction; in fact, Montreal municipal authorities placed a $100,000 fund at the disposal of the civil defence committee.
Unfortunately indeed, Mr. Chairman, I say this pointedly, between 1944 and 1957 a new administration took over in Montreal and deliberately abolished the civil defence committee under the pretense that $100,000 was not enough for a city like Montreal. I admit it was not very much but at least something was being done, citizens were learning how
Supply-Health and Welfare to evacuate homes, factories or public buildings in an orderly way and without panic.
The most simple definition of civil defence, which some find complicated, was given to us by Lieutenant R. Forand, co-ordinator for the city of Granby, in a talk he gave on February 8, 1954. Here is what he said about it: "Civil defence is the means whereby lives and property are safeguarded under atomic, biological or other attacks".
As you know, Mr. Chairman, Montreal is situated on an island. I therefore need not tell you that it would be a very attractive target for enemy air forces and you can imagine what would happen if Montrealers were not prepared to defend themselves, and what would be the responsibility of the federal government who would not have supplied Montreal citizens with the necessary and appropriate means of protection.
At the present time, the problem facing Montreal is the evacuation of the island. Present bridges are inadequate and this can easily be realized on week-ends when part of the population takes to the country to spend the two days of the week-end or to visit relatives. Bridges are crowded and you can only cross them by dint of patience, as traffic crawls along, when it is not altogether at a standstill.
Since 1957 Montreal has had an administration which has in mind a revival of a civil defence organization. Indeed, the appointment of a co-ordinator for the metropolis will no doubt be made soon.
Scientific developments brought about by nuclear warfare are such that the government should give civil defence an importance equal to that of national defence. I feel that if we are right in spending more than half of ' our national income for national defence, the government would certainly be well advised to spend in this regard more than the $7 million appearing in the estimates under the heading of civil defence.
A conference of municipalities will be held in the near future. This should provide the government with a fine opportunity to lay a civil defence plan before the municipalities. I must say at this point, speaking as a municipal councillor, that the minister may expect from the present mayor of Montreal co-operation of a kind which the former administration failed to receive from his predecessor.
This is a national program which should be financed by the federal government.

Supply-Health and Welfare That is why I submit that all expenses incurred by the municipalities in the implementation of a civil defence plan, should be met entirely by the federal government.
Before passing on to the next subject, Mr. Chairman, may I express a few thoughts on family allowances.
I would not like to miss this opportunity of suggesting once more to the government, as I have already done more than once during the present session, the possibility of increasing the amount of the family allowances. The minister knows that it was the Liberal government which instituted family allowances in 1945 and that these were raised on various occasions since that time, the more recent increase having been made, in fact, in the 1957 budget. During the last campaign, the leader of the opposition had undertaken to extend payment of family allowances to children still attending school until such time as they have reached the age of 18.
It is the least that we could do for our families and I would like to ask the minister, in his comments, to tell us what the government intends to do about increasing family allowances.
We must bear in mind that the cost of living has increased considerably since June 1957, especially for the three items of food, clothing and housing.
As there is unemployment in my constituency, a raise in family allowances is absolutely necessary. It would moreover be most welcome by all the citizens of Canada.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the minister has noted my suggestions and that he will at once take them into consideration.

speechtext: En resume, I simply attempted to draw some kind of comparison. As you know, there are many comparisons we could make tonight. But as the Chairman has said, I should return to the subject under discussion and I will accept his ruling because he is usually right. I would point out, however, that the hon. member for Quebec West argued about this very same thing this afternoon. I rather liked the way he talked. If I understood him correctly he was serving as sort of a porte-parole from Quebec in order to tell the minister they were short of hospital beds but that they were prepared to accept his will. If the hon. member for Quebec West thinks it is a good way of running a province to be always late and to be not prepared to take advantage of good legislation, I regret I cannot agree with him. Mind you, this legislation was passed by the former Liberal government and I congratulate the minister for not doing away with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: But it was brought into force by the Conservative government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is easy to blame the Quebec provincial government for not being in touch with the federal government, but I wonder if the minister is not himself to blame, for not doing anything about it. He appears to think the premier of that province does not exist. He treats him as a stranger. There has been no letter, no exchange of correspondence, no telegram. Nothing has been done. The result is that in the province of Quebec we pay taxes and do not get the advantage of the legislation, while the other provinces take advantage of it. The premier of Quebec, in the name of autonomy, is causing us to lose millions of dollars. We
Supply-Health and Welfare are going to pay for it and the province of Ontario and the other provinces will benefit from it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Did Quebec not get $19 million last year?

speechtext:
The hon. member for St.
Hyacinthe-Bagot gives me an idea. I remind him that the deputy minister of Quebec, Dr. Gregoire, said that 80 per cent of the population of Quebec could not take advantage of the hospitals in Quebec because they were too expensive and that there were only two types of people-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is no different from the other provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
-who could take advantage of them, namely those who had nothing and the rich. In the case of those who have nothing, their expenses are paid by the province and, of course, the ones who have money pay their own way.
According to the hon. member for Quebec West, the province is short of hospital beds and therefore cannot take advantage of this legislation. If the province is short of hospital beds it is because the hospitals are already full. If we take advantage of this legislation those who are already in the hospitals will also take advantage of it and besides that the hon. member's taxes will be used in his own province as well as in the province of Ontario. Therefore, I suggest to the minister that if they have no agreement or no contact with Quebec, let them put money aside as the former government did with respect to university grants. Before long we may have a new government in Quebec who will take charge of the province and accept the grants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity to say a few words on this very vitally important matter. First of all, I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare on the way he has directed this very important department of our government. I believe at the present time this department is the second highest spending department in the dominion, being superseded in this respect only by the Department of National Defence.
This department, Mr. Chairman, which is responsible for the welfare of so many of our citizens today, particularly the senior citizens of this country and the children, is now undertaking very great responsibility in the field of hospitalization. This is a major change which is taking place in our daily lives. Although the previous Liberal administration worked many years on this legislation it did not reach the point where

Supply

Health and Welfare the federal government became actively engaged in this field of endeavour. It was left for a Conservative government to expedite and to achieve this great social measure. In that regard the present minister has made a very important contribution, even toward advancing the effective date during this present session.
It is indeed regrettable that some members of the Liberal party saw fit to criticize this scheme which they themselves were promising for so many years-since 1919, I think- forgetting that the Liberals themselves were the architects of the present legislation and when they condemn it they merely add another nail to the coffin of the previous Liberal government and its inactivity and indifference toward this problem. The problem which the previous speaker mentioned is not a matter which has emanated from anything that has taken place in recent days; it is the result of something which was put on the statute books of this country by the previous Liberal administration, and the hon. member must realize that it was brought about by that regime.
As I said before, this is an excursion upon a new and untravelled road for the Canadian people. In the past there has been a state of affairs where people were content to obtain medical care in their own homes or by visiting their doctor's offices. Now the trend will be toward obtaining medical services in hospitals. I believe this is an important point because, in the past, many insurance companies, if not all, did not recognize the principle of hospitalization for investigation, a procedure which was undoubtedly responsible for keeping insurance premiums down to their present levels, although I must say that the medical profession was not altogether happy with this policy because undoubtedly there were many patients who required hospitalization for the purpose of finally and entirely ruling out the possibility of existing serious disease.
It is admitted that the hospital bed situation is not all that it could be, and just what the effect of including this extra service, this so-called investigation service, will have on the hospital facilities and on the insurance premiums only time will tell. Undoubtedly, there will be a great demand for the construction of more hospital facilities. These are problems which will become evident as time goes on and as the scheme is developed more fully. I believe the government is following a wise course in this regard, having in mind that some of the provinces have not as yet chosen to participate in the plan.
The Ontario scheme, which will become effective on January 1, 1959, includes all the hospital services necessary for the treatment
[Mr. Kucherepa.l

of an insured person who is admitted to hospital as an in-patient or, in an emergency.
I was very pleased to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson who touched on some vital problems dealing with the internal difficulties which face us in the hospitals across the country and to which I believe we must pay some attention lest the scheme should not function properly.
There is something else which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and of the committee, a matter which has given me some concern in the past. Over the years I have seen hospitals enlarged by additions of hundreds of beds to existing structures. Those buildings are located in what we might describe as the centrally populated areas of urban centres or they might be described in the field of civil defence as target areas. Although we were pleased with the developments in the last few days in international affairs, nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, I feel that we should undertake a long-range planning policy of decentralization of our hospital facilities, especially in our larger urban areas.
In the future we should take into account the problems of modern living. Yesterday we heard of plans being formulated for the removal of our government from this centre at a time when developments might take place which would necessitate that. Surely, Mr. Chairman, this principle applies just as much to the vital service of hospitalization which may mean the difference of life or death for many of our Canadian citizens. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the possibility of looking into this matter of whether we can in some way or another control the location of those hospital facilities in the future, having in mind that in the older cities of this country where there is a large development of hospital buildings we find that industrialization has taken place in those areas which might be construed as so-called target areas in the event of any future disaster.
I should also like to bring to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the problem which faces our people in the northern part of the country, especially the Eskimos. From what I can ascertain, the main problem in those areas which are so sparsely populated is to provide basic living conditions suitable to proper development of health measures. Our department does spend considerable funds in those areas. However, the results do not seem to be in keeping with the expenditures. It seems to me the basic problem here is to provide shelter for these people, especially for the children. The weather conditions there are severe, and thus housing becomes a major consideration, if we are to attain those

standards which are desirable, and which have indeed been obtained in other countries with a similar climate.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words regarding the contribution which Canada is making to the world health organization. I was gratified to hear the minister's statement in this regard. I believe that in this field of international relations we are not only making marvellous strides but we are also creating the kind of understanding which will bring about greater respect between the various countries of the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breion North and Victoria):
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to take a few minutes of the committee's time, Mr. Chairman, to bring to the attention of the minister a matter of extreme importance. I refer to the Disabled Persons Act. The administration of this act in the different provinces has rather confused me, especially in the province of Nova Scotia. It has been said that the regulations pertaining to this act are the same in all provinces, but from what I have seen and the information I have obtained, I feel this is incorrect. It appears that each province has its own idea of the definition of a permanently disabled person. It is quite true that there possibly would be some differences in the administration of the act because, as I understand it, each province has its own medical board which may interpret the clauses of the act in a different manner.
It seems that in some cases in the province of Nova Scotia the definition of permanently and totally disabled means that the individual concerned must be helpless or. in other words, practically a living log. A case in point comes to my mind at the moment. There was a person in my constituency who suffered a paralytic stroke about a year ago. He was confined to the hospital for a period of months, but eventually was discharged and returned to his home. There was not anything further that could be done for him so far as hospitalization or medication was concerned. The man was paralysed all down one side of his body, and his other arm was affected to the extent that he had to be fed. He was confined to bed in his own home. However, in spite of his condition, his application for a disabled person's pension was rejected. I still have his file, but it will not be necessary to give it any further consideration because unfortunately this poor man passed away a few weeks ago.
Just what is a disabled person? I have another case of a young man, 34 years of age, who suffered a severe accident with his father's mowing machine when he was four years old. He is unable to walk. Today he is
Supply-Health and Welfare able to crawl around with iron straps on his legs in order to support his ankles. The extent of his capability is that if he is carried out to the fields he can sit down and pull some weeds with his hands. This man has tried for two years to obtain a disabled person's pension without success, despite his tragic condition.
I do not wish to take up too much of the committee's time, but I should like to relate another very sad case. This concerns a man I have known since we were boys together. His left leg and arm have been withered since birth, so he has a difficult time in getting around. This is bad enough, but he is also subject to epileptic fits and has, on occasion, been found on the streets suffering from these fits. He has not any parents living and is surviving upon what sympathetic friends have been able to give him. His application for a disabled person's pension has been rejected on several occasions.
Since the cost of this pension is borne jointly by the provincial and federal governments, I feel that the instances which I have just related should be brought to the attention of the committee. I should like to ask the minister if it would not be possible to have a conference of provincial medical boards and his department with a view to having this act more uniformly and more leniently administered. In my opinion the act is interpreted too stringently in Nova Scotia so far as the definition of permanently and totally disabled is concerned. I think I have illustrated this fact in a small way. In closing, I would appeal to the minister for a relaxation of the regulations governing this act so that many people in these unfortunate circumstances such as I have mentioned would benefit thereby.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I want to say only a few words to bring to the attention of the committee, and of the minister in particular, the work done by the society for emotionally disturbed children. According to a pamphlet published by the society, until quite recently many of these children were considered mentally retarded because of their lack of response to people. However, medical science now diagnoses these children as suffering from a psychosis.
The society for emotionally disturbed children was formed in 1956 in Montreal by a small group of parents of such children. It has since grown to include many persons who have no personal interest but who do recognize that without the aid of public authorities these children would be doomed to a tragic fate. The society needs more funds to help fulfil its objectives. There are no quick cures or methods to help emotionally disturbed children. They usually

Supply-Health and Welfare require long term therapeutic treatment in a private environment. In order to provide these conditions special schools and specially trained personnel are needed, both of which are difficult to obtain. Because of the nature of this illness many of the children cannot fit into classes in the public schools and are, therefore, left without any schooling whatever.
I submit that the Department of National Health and Welfare should find the means to give financial support to this work of the society for emotionally disturbed children. I am sure the minister will take this request into consideration, and in the name of the society and the children involved I thank him.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like first of all, Mr. Chairman, to thank the many members who have spoken this afternoon and this evening for their helpful ideas and their kind words. I will admit that sometimes 1 have received congratulations, while at other times there have been differences of opinion expressed. I hope to answer satisfactorily those questions which have been asked of me, and I trust I do not answer them in too political a manner. If, when I am finished, I seem to have missed certain questions which members may have asked, I can only apologize for that. I trust that they will bring them up on the items to which they apply. I do feel, however, that there has been a good study of the department's estimates this afternoon. This shows that hon. members are interested in the department, and for that I am grateful.
May I say, first of all, that I am going to leave unanswered those questions having to do with civil defence until that item comes before us. I think I mentioned at the start of my remarks this morning that I did have a short statement to make on civil defence when that item is reached. As a consequence, I would prefer to get to that point before discussing civil defence any further, and at that time I will endeavour to answer the questions which were asked.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres -those two in particular-mentioned the fact that the annual report for my department had as yet not been tabled. That is quite true. That delay is accounted for by the simple fact that there are two unavoidable and unexpected vacancies on the senior staff of the information services division of my department. I fully expect that this report will be tabled within two or three weeks. It is my regret that it has not been done thus far, I might add that there were some difficulties also in having the report printed.


The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River spoke about Salk vaccine. I would point out that the government is now prepared to extend financial assistance in the provision of Salk vaccine to adults. As in the past, federal contributions would amount to one-half the cost of the vaccine, the remainder to be met by the province. Incidentally, I may say I have noticed a couple of newspaper reports recently which would seem to indicate that the provinces were possibly footing the full cost of this vaccine. That is not quite so. The government is sharing this cost 50-50. Since information on the number of children vaccinated is incomplete, particularly with respect to some of the larger provinces, it is difficult to specify a firm figure of those vaccinated. It is estimated, however, that more than 5,200,000 persons have received at least one or more doses of poliomyelitis vaccine by June 1, 1958. I think that is rather commendable.
The hon. member also inquired about cancer research. I would make a short reply in this respect. Prior to 1948-49 fundamental research on cancer was limited in Canada owing to lack of facilities, qualified research personnel and assured long term support. Although the national research council allocated grants for short term projects, applications received were not commensurate to the extent of the problem. I should like to point out that in 1957-58, 75 grants and 16 research fellowships were awarded totalling $630,000. For the current fiscal year 83 grants and 17 fellowships and associates have been awarded totalling some $820,000.
Hospital insurance has been in many members' thinking this afternoon and this evening. I think that during the discussion of amendments to the act some weeks ago this subject was covered fairly fully. I would express again my opinion as to the definite situation that exists. If all the provinces come in there will be ten different, distinct hospital schemes. As long as these schemes come within the context of the federal act, nothing else is required. As to the situation with regard to T.B. and mental hospitals-I was asked this question earlier-I have replied many times in the past. The situation is still unchanged. As far as the government is concerned, these ten schemes which would be in force if all ten provinces were within the hospital scheme would be different for special reasons. There are different forces in effect in different provinces. We do not wish to dictate to the provinces exactly what scheme they should institute. As long as their scheme is within the over-all context of our act, that is all that is required.

I would point out-I think hon. members on the opposite side of the house might realize this fact-that this act which is in force today is exactly the same act which was brought in by an administration which at that time was a Liberal administration in April, 1957. The only change that has been made since then is that we have moved forward the possible starting date from January 1, 1959 to July 1, 1958. In other words, this act is exactly the same in its approach to the problem of hospital insurance across Canada. As for myself, I feel that it would ill behoove us at this stage to try to dictate to the provinces exactly what they should have. We are leaving it open to them to present their scheme as they see fit provided it meets our over-all act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question at this point?

speechtext: I indicated to the committee this morning that I was privileged to be one of the federal delegates with the then minister of national health and welfare -I was representing the finance department at the time, I think-when we were meeting with the provincial officials, I think the provincial treasurers and ministers of health, in 1955 and 1956 in two conferences. I think our estimate at the moment is that if all the provinces were in the actual cost would be in the neighbourhood of $210 million. I may say quite frankly that we shall be able to tell you a great deal more closely after one year of operation. There is no doubt about that.

speechtext: Does the minister believe they are all in his department?

Yes. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River inquired about the advertising by our department, and I would point out that there is $550,000 in the primary for educational and informational materials. There were other comments this afternoon with respect to publications, particularly the child training booklets which are distributed mainly to hospitals and schools throughout the provinces. There is no active advertising campaign as such. This is purely an endeavour made in the form of booklets and other educational media.
The hon. member for Timmins said that in his view at least the department had no vision, and he appeared to think that this is illustrated by our hospital insurance plan. My approach, and that of the government, to this plan has been a very simple one. This act was brought into being as at April, 1957, and when I took office one year ago today, I said that it was my ambition to put this legislation into effect. This has materialized purely by the fact that five provinces now have it in force and we expect greater participation as of January 1, 1959. I wish to repeat a statement I have made on previous occasions to the effect that after this scheme has been in force for a year or two I will be very happy to consider whatever suggestions are made to me for possible amendments. I do not think any piece of legislation as complex as this one could be perfect as a result of our first effort, and I am convinced that amendments will have to be made. Some adjustments have already been made in the agreements between the provinces-not the agreements themselves but the regulations- in order to meet certain conditions. We will be quite happy to consider further amendments to the legislation when it is shown that there are weaknesses in the act as it presently exists.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Just on that point, my hon. friend and his associates some time ago made up their minds, of course, with respect to the desirability of including in the 50-50 share the cost of operating tubercular and mental institutions. Would the minister make some comment on that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

I have said that the situation in that respect has been unchanged since the time when the amendment went through, at which time I made my last statement on the subject in this house. The advancement of the date of the possible starting from January 1, 1959 to July 1, 1958 was at that time and, as I said earlier this evening, the situation remains the same. Mental and tuberculosis hospitals are not 
under consideration at the moment. I think that answers my hon. friend's question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does the minister think that the fact that this matter has been shelved is in any way responsible for the fact that to date the province of Quebec does not appear to be very interested in participating in this scheme?

I do not think so, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for the Yukon mentioned the use of mobile health units in the north, which units are actually trailers. I found that hon. member's speech just a little bit political, and I think I am entitled to reply-

speechtext: By $42 million in 1947.

In connection with family allowances, I think it is well to note that these suggestions made on the floor of the house are sometimes made in what might be described as a rather carefree spirit; such as, "Well, what does it matter, we will just mention it", and that sort of thing. For every one dollar increase monthly there would be required an additional annual outlay of $70 million. I hope the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres can balance his request for increased family allowances with the suggestion that perhaps we had increased old age security benefits too much.

I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Jasper-Edson for his definite interest shown in the hospital insurance scheme. I welcome his remarks. We all accept the fact that the medical profession has accepted its responsibility in regard to the hospital scheme. The hon. member mentioned uniformity. Here again I mention that I do not feel that we should have complete uniformity across the country. speechtext:
Before vote 256 carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a brief statement on Canada's civil defence effort during the past fiscal year.
At the outset, I would remind hon. members that the dominion government has felt it advisable to take a new look at our plans and activities in this field in view primarily of recent changes in the nature of the threat confronting this and other countries of the world. As I announced to the house on June 11, Lieutenant-General Howard D. Graham has agreed to undertake a comprehensive survey of all aspects of Canada's
Supply-Health and Welfare civil defence policy and program with particular reference to the implications which intercontinental ballistic missiles may have on these arrangements.
As far as the fiscal year 1957-58 is concerned, I believe it is fair to say that steady progress has been made in civil defence planning and training. In the matter of overall policy we have continued to follow the previously established approach of developing and testing plans for the orderly evacuation, on short notice, of certain urban target areas in the event that a nuclear attack should appear imminent. At the same time, advances in space travel and missile techniques have been watched closely and their possible impact on civil defence preparations kept constantly under review. While our planning in this field is still based on meeting the present threat of the piloted bomber it has also looked forward to the time when the ICBM can be expected to alter the strategic pattern of enemy attack.
Turning to specific developments, I might mention the initiation of a national civil defence day which received substantial public support last October and which will again be observed on September 19 next.
Another advance worthy of note is the increased emphasis which has been given to armed service co-operation with civil defence authorities. As hon. members are aware, the training of the militia during the current year is being concentrated on civil defence. In this connection my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, has explained that this shift of emphasis does not mean that the militia will take over civil defence or that civil defence will take over the militia. It simply represents another step towards implementing the established policy that the armed services, co-ordinated by the army, will come to the aid of civil defence authorities in the event of a nuclear attack. Since civil defence is of necessity organized on a local basis of self-help, with few, if any, mobile reserves, the main tasks of the armed services will be to provide mobile support groups and assistance with technical units and equipment to local civilian effort, both during evacuation and for subsequent operations.
The problems associated with armed service-civil defence co-operation were discussed in March of this year when a special conference was held at the national civil defence college at Arnprior. The results of these meetings, which were attended by senior officers of the three armed services, officials of federal, provincial and municipal civil defence organizations, as well as by representatives from other federal departments, were most encouraging and are now under careful study.

Supply-Health and Welfare
A further indication of increasing armed service-civil defence co-operation can be found in the mounting numbers of military personnel being trained at the Arnprior college. As against some 200 attending courses in 1955, more than 800 members of the armed services have received some kind of training at the college during the first six months of 1958.
As far as other training is concerned, I might say that more than 3,500 instructors and key workers attended courses at Arnprior during the past fiscal year, bringing the total of such persons trained under federal auspices to over 17,000. These, in turn, have provided instruction to over 135,000 additional persons in the provinces or municipalities.
In the realm of financing of our civil defence program, I would draw the attention of hon. members to two points. First, of the $7,054,085 originally budgeted for 1957-58, only $5,885,738 was actually made available. This was due to the fact that in the absence of parliamentary appropriation the money had to be provided through governor general's warrants which were limited to estimated cash needs. This explains what might appear to be a substantial increase in our civil defence budget for 1958-59. While representing an increment of $1,141,983 over the estimated cash needs for last year, our current estimate of $7,027,721 is, in fact, $26,384 less than was originally budgeted for 1957-58.
A second point which should be mentioned in this connection is the lapsed balance of $1,896,134 of the $5,885,738 made available last year. This resulted largely from unliquidated commitments in the medical stockpiling program and from the fact that most of the provinces underspent their quotas under the financial assistance program. In budgeting again at the $7 million level, the government is hopeful that the provinces will be in a position in the current fiscal year to take full advantage of the federal funds available.
With respect to the financial assistance program-which at $2 million is the second largest item in the civil defence estimates- an important modification was introduced effective April 1, 1958. Prior to that date municipalities were reimbursed for only 25 per cent of their expenditures on approved civil defence projects if the province did not participate. As a result of the change the federal government may now contribute 50 per cent of municipal expenditures regardless of whether or not the province makes any contribution. In taking this step the government hopes to give new impetus to


local civil defence efforts which, of course, form the underlying basis of all action in this field.
There have been two developments since the end of the last fiscal year which I should also like to mention. Early in May, a nationwide exercise entitled "Co-operation II" was carried out with a good deal of success. Involving most of the provinces, many municipalities, the armed services, the R.C.M.P., as well as the United States civil defence headquarters at Battle Creek, Michigan, this project afforded an excellent opportunity to analyse much of our civil defence planning. It also brought to light situations requiring further study with a view to improving the effectiveness of organizations at all three levels of responsibility.
At the end of May, I had the pleasure of taking part, with Governor Leo A. Hoegh, head of the newly-formed United States office of defence and civilian mobilization, and other United States civil defence officials, in the sixth meeting of the joint United States-Canada civil defence committee. I found this a most satisfying session at which substantial progress was made in such matters as plans to ensure the continuation of government in the event of an international emergency, technical developments in the provision of shelter against radioactive fallout, and practical application of the "no border" policy.
Looking to the future, I have already mentioned Lieutenant General Graham's far-reaching survey of civil defence policies and programs. Another forthcoming development of note will be the meeting of the federal-provincial civil defence advisory committee which has not been convened since 1954. The dominion government is most anxious to revive this important body and feels that the session scheduled for next October should prove extremely useful, particularly in view of the fact that new ministers responsible for civil defence have recently been appointed at both federal and provincial levels. Co-operation between federal and provincial governments is, of course, one of the key elements in Canada's civil defence activities and we are convinced that this committee can play a really vital role in furthering progress in this regard.

1.	Did a collision occur between the C.P.S. ferry Princess Helene and pilot boat No. 6 off Saint John harbour on August 8, 1958?
2.	If so, what is the official report of the Department of Transport regarding responsibility and damage?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
1.	A minor collision occurred in the approach channel to Saint John harbour on August 8, 1958, between the C.P.R. ferry Princess Helene and pilot boat No. 6.
2.	Both vessels were proceeding with caution in dense fog so that contact and resulting damage were very light. Repairs are estimated to cost about $330 for pilot boat No. 6 and about $700 for Princess Helene. The seaworthiness of neither ship was affected.
